questions.question: For the NMOSFET in the circuit shown, the threshold voltage is \(V_{th}\) , where \(V_{th} > 0\). The source voltage \(V_{SS}\) is varied from 0 to \(V_{DD}\). Neglecting the channel length modulation, the drain current \(I_D\) as a function of \(V_{SS}\) is represented by
questions.explanation: In the given figure, since gate is shorted to drain ,the MOSFET is in saturation. Current in saturation is given by \[I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_{TH})^2\] We have \(V_{GS} = V_{DD} - V_{SS}\) and let \(\frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} = K_n\), then \[I_D = K_n(V_{DD} - V_{TH} - V_{SS})^2\] Let \(V_{DD} - V_{TH} = A = \text{constant}\) \[\Rightarrow I_D = K_n(A - V_{SS})^2\] This is equation of parabola For \(V_{SS} = 0, I_D = K_n A (\text{maximum})\) and for \(V_{SS} = V_{DD} - V_{TH}, I_D = 0\) \[\boxed{\text{Option (A) is correct.}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, both the enhancement mode NMOS transistors have the following characteristics: \(k_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L) = 1\,\text{mA/V}^2\) ; \(V_{TN} = 1\,\text{V}\) Assume that the channel length modulation parameter \(\lambda\) is zero and body is shorted to source. The minimum supply voltage \(V_{DD}\) (in volts) needed to ensure that transistor \(M_1\) operates in saturation mode of operation is _________.
questions.explanation: Given circuit is , We observe that MOSFET \(M_2\) is diode connected so, \(V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{Th}\). So, \(M_2\) is operating in the saturation region. \[\text{So, } I = (I_{DS})_2 = \frac{\mu_n C_{ox}}{2} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_{Th})^2 (1 + \lambda V_{DS}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) (V_{DD} - x - 1)^2 \quad \dots 1)\] For \(M_1\) to be in Saturation, \(V_{DS1}\) must be greater than or equal to \(V_{GS1} - V_{th}\), i.e. \[x \ge 2 - 1 = 1\] \[\Rightarrow x \ge 1 \Rightarrow x_{min} = 1 \quad \dots 2)\] \[I = (I_{DS})_1 = \frac{\mu_n C_{ox}}{2} \frac{W}{L} \left[ (V_{GS1} - V_{Th})^2 (1 + \lambda V_{DS1}) \right] = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) (2 - 1)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\,\text{mA} \quad \dots 3)\] Now equating Equations 1) & 3), we get; \[\Rightarrow \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) (V_{DD} - x - 1)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\] \[\Rightarrow (V_{DD} - x - 1)^2 = 1\] \[\Rightarrow V_{DD} = x + 2.\] Using Equation-(2) which says that \(x \ge 1\). So, \(V_{DD} \ge 3\,\text{volts}\). \[\boxed{V_{DD(\text{min})}=3\,\text{V}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A MOSFET in saturation has a drain current of \(1\,\text{mA}\) for \(V_{DS} = 0.5\,\text{V}\). If the channel length modulation coefficient is \(0.05\,\text{V}^{-1}\), the output resistance (in \(\text{k}\Omega\)) of the MOSFET is _________.
questions.explanation:
Given: \(I_D = 1\,\text{mA}\) Channel length modulation coefficient \(= 0.05\,\text{V}^{-1}\) The drain current when the MOSFET is in saturation is given by: \[I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) \times (V_{GS} - V_T)^2\] The output resistance (\(r_o\)) is given by: \[r_o = \frac{V_A}{I_D}\] \[V_A = \frac{1}{\lambda}\] where \(\lambda = \text{Channel length parameter}\) \[V_A = \frac{1}{\lambda} = 20\] \[r_o = \frac{V_A}{I_D} = \frac{20}{1\,\text{mA}} = 20\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[\boxed{\text{The output impedance is }20\,\text{k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • It is mathematically defined as \(r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D}\), where \(\lambda\) is the channel length modulation coefficient.
  • By introducing the Early voltage \(V_A = \frac{1}{\lambda}\), the equation simplifies to \(r_o = \frac{V_A}{I_D}\), which makes it analogous to BJT output resistance calculations.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The current in an enhancement mode NMOS transistor biased in saturation mode was measured to be \(1\,\text{mA}\) at a drain-source voltage of \(5\,\text{V}\). When the drain-source voltage was increased to \(6\,\text{V}\) while keeping gate-source voltage same, the drain current increased to \(1.02\,\text{mA}\). Assume that drain to source saturation voltage is much smaller than the applied drain-source voltage. The channel length modulation parameter \(\lambda\) (in \(V^{-1}\)) is _________.
questions.explanation:
Saturation Current in an enhancement mode N-MOS is given as: \[I_{DS} = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} \times \frac{W}{L} [V_{GS} - V_T]^2 (1 + \lambda \cdot V_{DS})\] Case-I:
\(V_{DS} = 5\,\text{V}, I_{DS} = 1\,\text{mA}\) \[1 = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_T)^2 (1 + 5\lambda) \quad \dots (1)\] Case-II:
\(V_{DS} = 6\,\text{V}, I_{DS} = 1.02\,\text{mA}\) \[1.02 = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_T)^2 (1 + 6\lambda) \quad \dots (2)\] Dividing Equation (1) by Equation (2), we get, \[\frac{1}{1.02} = \frac{1 + 5\lambda}{1 + 6\lambda}\] \[\Rightarrow 1 + 6\lambda = 1.02(1 + 5\lambda)\] \[\Rightarrow 1 + 6\lambda = 1.02 + 5.1\lambda\] \[\Rightarrow 0.9\lambda = 0.02\] \[\boxed{\lambda = \frac{2}{90} \approx 0.0222}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, assume that the opamp is ideal. The bridge output voltage \(V_0\) (in mV) for \(\delta = 0.05\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is shown below, From virtual ground concept, \[V_+ = V_- = 1\,\text{V}\] Since op-amp terminals draw no current, same current flows through \(100\,\Omega\) and \(50\,\Omega\) resistors. \[I_{50\Omega} = I_{100\Omega} = \frac{1}{50}\,\text{A}\] Applying KVL in the loop shown in figure, \[-V_0 + \frac{1}{100}[250(1+\delta) - 250(1-\delta)] = 0\] \[V_0 = \frac{1}{100}[250(1+\delta) - 250(1-\delta)]\] \[V_0 = \frac{1}{100} \times 500\delta\] \[V_0 = 5\delta = 5 \times 0.05 = 0.25\,\text{V}\] \[V_0 = 250\,\text{mV}\] \[\boxed{\text{The bridge output voltage} V_0 \text{ is } 250 \text{ mV}}\].
Key points
  • Bridge Circuit Symmetry: Due to the symmetry of the bridge resistances (\(250(1+\delta) + 250(1-\delta) = 500\,\Omega\) on both branches), the total current entering the bottom node divides equally between the two branches.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure has an ideal opamp. The oscillation frequency and the condition to sustain the oscillations, respectively, are
questions.explanation: Given circuit is, The circuit is a Wein bridge oscillator. It consists of amplifier part and a frequency selective feedback network. The amplifier is a non-inverting amplifier whose gain is, \[A=\frac{V_{out}}{V_f}=1+\frac{R_1}{R_2}\] The feedback factor is given by, \[\beta(s)=\frac{V_f}{V_{out}}=\frac{Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}\] where, \[Z_1=R\parallel \frac{1}{2sC}=\frac{R\cdot \frac{1}{2sC}}{R+\frac{1}{2sC}}=\frac{R}{1+2sRC}\] \[Z_2=2R+\frac{1}{sC}=\frac{1+2sRC}{sC}\] \[\beta(s)=\frac{\frac{R}{1+2sRC}}{\frac{R}{1+2sRC}+\frac{1+2sRC}{sC}}\] \[\beta(s)=\frac{RsC}{RsC+(1+2sRC)^2}\] \[\beta(s)=\frac{sRC}{sRC+(1+2sRC)^2}\] \[\beta(s)=\frac{sRC}{sRC+1+4sRC+4s^2R^2C^2}\] \[\beta(s)=\frac{sRC}{1+5sRC+4s^2R^2C^2}\] Put \(s=j\omega\), \[\beta(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega CR}{1+5j\omega RC+4(j\omega)^2R^2C^2}\] \[\beta(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega CR}{1-4\omega^2R^2C^2+j5\omega RC}\] From Barkhausen criteria, the total phase shift should be zero, for which \(\beta\) should have zero phase. Hence \[1-4\omega^2R^2C^2=0\] \[4\omega^2R^2C^2=1\] \[\omega^2=\frac{1}{4R^2C^2}\] \[\omega_0=\frac{1}{2RC}\] From Bark Hausen Criterion, loop gain should be 1. So, \(A\beta = 1\), we get \[A\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)=1\qquad \because \text{ at }\omega=\omega_0, \beta(\omega_0)=1/5\] \[1 + \frac{R_1}{R_2} = 5 \implies R_1 = 4R_2\] \[\boxed{\text{(D)}\quad \omega_0=\frac{1}{2RC},\qquad R_1=4R_2}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, \(V_0 = V_{0A}\) for switch SW in position \(A\) and \(V_0 = V_{0B}\) for SW in position \(B\). Assume that the opamp is ideal. The value of \(\dfrac{V_{0B}}{V_{0A}}\) is ________.
questions.explanation: When switch is in position A : From virtual ground concept, \[V_+ = V_- = V_a\] Applying KCL at inverting terminal, \[\frac{V_a - 5}{1} + \frac{V_a - V_{0A}}{1} = 0\] \[V_{0A} = 2V_a - 5\] Apply voltage division rule at non-inverting terminal, \[V_a = \frac{1}{1 + 1} \times 1 = 0.5\,\text{V}\] \[\therefore V_{0A} = 2 \times 0.5 - 5 = -4\,\text{V}\] When switch is at position B : Non-inverting input, \(V_a = 0\,\text{V}\) and due to virtual short inverting terminal voltage also becomes 0. Applying KCL at inverting terminal, \[\frac{0 - 1}{1} + \frac{0 - 5}{1} + \frac{0 - V_{0B}}{1} = 0\] \[-1 - 5 - V_{0B} = 0\] \[V_{0B} = -6\,\text{V}\] Therefore, \[{\frac{V_{0B}}{V_{0A}} = \frac{-6}{-4} = 1.5}\] \[\boxed{\frac{V_{0B}}{V_{0A}} = 1.5}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the bistable circuit shown, the ideal opamp has saturation levels of \(\pm 5\text{ V}\). The value of \(R_1\) (in \(\text{k}\Omega\)) that gives a hysteresis width of \(500\text{ mV}\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given, (i) Saturation level \(= \pm V_{sat} = \pm 5\,\text{V}\) (ii) Hysteresis width, \(V_H = 500\,\text{mV}\) Given circuit is, The circuit is a non inverting Schmitt trigger circuit and, op-amp with positive feedback does not follow virtual ground concept. By using superposition theorem, voltage \(V_+\) is given by, \[V_+ = \left. \frac{V_{in} \times R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \right|_{V_{out}=0} + \left. \frac{V_{out} \times R_1}{R_1 + R_2} \right|_{V_{in}=0}\] Case 1 : When \(V_{out} = +V_{sat}\), Then \[V_+ = \frac{V_{in}R_2}{R_1 + R_2} + \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_1 + R_2}\] \(V_{out} = +V_{sat}\) if \(V_+ > 0\) i.e. \[\frac{V_{in}R_2}{R_1 + R_2} + \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_1 + R_2} > 0\] \[V_{in} > -V_{sat}\frac{R_1}{R_2} \quad \dots\text{(i)}\] Case 2 : When \(V_{out} = -V_{sat}\) Then \[V_+ = \frac{V_{in}R_2}{R_1 + R_2} - \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_1 + R_2}\] \(V_{out} = -V_{sat}\) if \(V_+ < 0\) \[\frac{V_{in}R_2}{R_1 + R_2} - \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_1 + R_2} < 0\] \[V_{in} < \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_2} \quad \dots\text{(ii)}\] Transfer characteristics is shown below, where, \(V_1 = \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_2}\) and \(V_2 = \frac{-V_{sat}R_1}{R_2}\) Hysteresis voltage or width is given by, \[V_H = V_1 - V_2 = \frac{V_{sat}R_1}{R_2} - \left( \frac{-V_{sat}R_1}{R_2} \right)\] \[V_H = 2V_{sat}\frac{R_1}{R_2}\] \[0.5 = 2 \times 5 \times \frac{R_1}{20}\] \[\boxed{R_1 = 1\,\text{k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • Hysteresis Width (\(V_H\)): The voltage difference between the upper and lower threshold levels (\(V_{UTP}\) and \(V_{LTP}\)). For this specific configuration, it is determined by the ratio of the feedback resistors: \(V_H = 2 V_{sat} \left( \frac{R_1}{R_2} \right)\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: Assuming that the opamp in the circuit shown below is ideal, the output voltage \(V_o\) (in volts) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is shown below, From the above circuit, \[V_+ = 1\,\text{V} , \ V_- = 0\,\text{V}\] Virtual ground concept is not applicable when both input terminals are known. So, ideal Op-Amp act as a comparator circuit. From figure, \[V_+ > V_-\] So, \[V_0 = +V_{sat} = +12\,\text{V}\] Hence, the output voltage \(V_0\) is 12 V. \[\boxed{V_0 = 12\text{ V}}\]
Key points
  • When negative feedback is disabled (in this case, by hardwiring the inverting terminal to ground), the op-amp operates in open-loop mode and acts as a comparator.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown using an ideal opamp, the 3-dB cut-off frequency (in Hz) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Circuit can be redrawn as, The circuit has negative feedback so using virtual short concept \(V_-=V_x\) From non-inverting terminal : Change the circuit in transform domain Voltage \(V_x\) is given by, \[V_x = \frac{\frac{1}{Cs}}{R + \frac{1}{Cs}} \times V_i(s) = \frac{V_i(s)}{1 + RCs}\] Using KCL at inverting terminal, \[\frac{V_x}{R} + \frac{V_x - V_0(s)}{R} = 0\] \[V_0(s) = 2V_x = \frac{2V_i(s)}{1 + RCs}\] Voltage gain is given by, \[A(s) = \frac{V_0(s)}{V_i(s)} = \frac{2}{1 + RCs}\] Put \(s = j\omega\) in above equation, \[A(j\omega) = \frac{2}{1 + j\omega RC}\] \[|A(j\omega)| = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2}}\] At \(\omega = 0\), \(|A(j0)| = A_0 = 2\) At 3-dB cut-off frequency, \[|A(j\omega_c)| = \frac{A_0}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\frac{2}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega_c RC)^2}} = \frac{A_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\frac{4}{1 + (\omega_c RC)^2} = 2\] \[2 = 1 + (\omega_c RC)^2\] \[1 = (\omega_c RC)^2\] \[\omega_c RC = \pm 1\] Taking the positive value for frequency, \[\omega_c = \frac{1}{RC}\] \[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\] \[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10^4 \times 10^{-7}} = 159.15\,\text{Hz}\]
Method 2
The circuit in Method-1 can be redrawn in the form of a standard first order low pass filter as, For first order LPF, 3-dB cut-off frequency is given by, \[f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10\,\text{k}\Omega \times 0.1\,\mu\text{F}}\] \[f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10^4 \times 0.1 \times 10^{-6}} = 159.15\,\text{Hz}\]
\[\boxed{f_H= 159.15\text{ Hz}}\]
Key points
  • First-Order Low-Pass Filter (LPF): The input RC network forms a simple low-pass filter. The 3-dB cutoff frequency (the frequency at which the power drops to half its midband value, or voltage gain drops by \(1/\sqrt{2}\)) is fundamentally governed by \(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, assume that the opamp is ideal. If the gain (\(v_o / v_{in}\)) is \(-12\), the value of R (in \(\text{k}\Omega\)) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given, \(\dfrac{V_0}{V_i} = -12\) Given circuit is shown below, From virtual ground concept, \[V_+ = V_- = 0\,\text{V}\] Applying KCL at inverting terminal, \[\frac{0 - V_i}{10} + \frac{0 - V_x}{10} = 0\] \[V_x = -V_i \quad \dots\text{(i)}\] Applying KCL at \(V_x\), \[\frac{V_x}{10} + \frac{V_x}{R} + \frac{V_x - V_0}{10} = 0\] \[-\frac{V_i}{10} - \frac{V_i}{R} - \frac{V_i}{10} = \frac{V_0}{10} \quad \text{[From equation (i)]}\] \[-1 - \frac{10}{R} - 1 = \left( \frac{V_0}{V_i} \right)\] \[-\frac{10}{R} - 2 = -12 \quad \left[ \text{Given : } \frac{V_0}{V_i} = -12 \right]\] \[\frac{10}{R} = 10 \implies R = 1\,\text{k}\Omega\] Hence, the value of \(R\) is 1 k\(\Omega\). \[\boxed{R=1\text{k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • Using a T-network in the feedback loop allows for the realization of high voltage gains without requiring extremely large feedback resistor values.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, \(I_1 = 80 \text{ mA}\) and \(I_2 = 4 \text{ mA}\). Transistors \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are identical. Assume that the thermal voltage \(V_T\) is \(26 \text{ mV}\) at \(27 ^{\circ}\text{C}\). At \(50 ^{\circ}\text{C}\), the value of the voltage \(V_{12} = V_1 - V_2 \text{ (in mV)}\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given \(I_1 = 80\) mA, \(I_2 = 4\) mA and \(V_T = 26\) mV at \(27^o\). The given circuit is, Applying KVL we get, \[-V_{BE1} + V_{12} + V_{BE2} = 0\] \[\therefore V_{12} = V_{BE1} - V_{BE2}\] But \(I_1 \propto e^{\frac{V_{BE1}}{V_T}}\) and \(I_2 \propto e^{\frac{V_{BE2}}{V_T}}\) \[\frac{I_1}{I_2} = e^{\left( \frac{V_{BE1} - V_{BE2}}{V_T} \right)} = \frac{80}{4}=20\] \[\therefore V_{BE1} - V_{BE2} = V_T \ln 20\] We know \(V_T \propto T\)(in Kelvin). Therefore \[V_{T_{50^o}} (27+273) = V_{T_{27^o}}(50+273)\implies V_{T_{50^o}}=\frac{323\times 26\text{ mV}}{300}=28 \text{ mV}\] \[\therefore V_{12}= V_{BE1} - V_{BE2} = V_T \ln 20 = {83.88\,\text{mV}}\] \[\boxed{V_{12}=83.88 \text{ mV}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship between collector current and base-emitter voltage in a BJT is proportional to \(e^{\frac{V_{BE}}{V_T}}\).
  • Thermal voltage can be calculated using the relationship \(\frac{V_{T_1}}{V_{T_2}}=\frac{T_1}{T_2}\) where temperature is in Kelvin.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For the voltage regulator circuit shown, the input voltage (\(V_{in}\)) is \(20 \text{ V} \pm 20\%\) and the regulated output voltage (\(V_{out}\)) is \(10 \text{ V}\). Assume the opamp to be ideal. For a load \(R_L\) drawing \(200 \text{ mA}\), the maximum power dissipation in \(Q_1\) (in Watts) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given \[V_{in} = 20 \pm 20\%,\, V_0 = 10\,\text{V},\, I_{L} = 200\,\text{mA}\] \[V_{in} = 20 \pm 20\% = [24\,\text{V}, 16\,\text{V}]\] Given circuit is, For maximum power dissipation, we consider maximum \(V_{in} \text{ i.e, } 24\,\text{V}\) From the circuit, we have: \[V_{CE} = V_{in} - V_{out} = 24 - 10 = 14\,\text{V}\] Applying virtual ground concept, we get: \[V_n = V_p = 4\,\text{V}\] So: \[I_{R2} = \frac{4}{10} = 0.4\,\text{mA}\] No current will flow through the op-amp terminals, i.e. \[I_1 = I_{R2} = 0.4\,\text{mA} \quad \text{and} \quad I_{L} = 200\,\text{mA}\] \[I_E = I_1 + I_{L}\] \[I_E = 200.4\,\text{mA}\] \[\therefore I_C = I_E = 200.4\,\text{mA}\] Now: \[P(Q_{1max}) = V_{CE} \times I_C\] \[= 14 \times 200.4 \times 10^{-3}\] \[\boxed{P_{Q1} = {2.80}\,\text{Watt}}\]
Key points
  • The power dissipated by a series pass transistor is calculated as the product of the collector-emitter voltage (\(V_{CE}\)) and the collector current (\(I_C\)).
  • To find the maximum power dissipation, the upper limit of the input voltage tolerance must be considered.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the AC equivalent circuit shown, the two BJTs are biased in active region and have identical parameters with \(\beta \gg 1\). The open circuit small signal voltage gain is approximately ________.
questions.explanation:
In the given circuit, trans-conductance for both the transistors will be the same and will be equal to \(g_m\), as the transistors are identical. For the given circuit, the upper transistor acts as a diode-connected load and the resistance seen into any of its terminals is equal to \(1/g_m\). The circuit can be redrawn as, The above circuit is a simple common emitter amplifier whose voltage gain is given by, \[A_v = -g_m\times (r_0||R_c) = -g_m \times \left(r_0||\frac{1}{g_m}\right)\] Since \(r_0 \gg 1/g_m\implies r_0||(1/g_m)\approx 1/g_m\) \[A_v = -g_m\times \frac{1}{g_m} = -1\]
Key points
  • A transistor with its base and collector shorted acts as a diode-connected load, providing a small-signal resistance of approximately \(\frac{1}{g_m}\).
  • The intrinsic output resistance (\(r_o\)) of a transistor is typically much larger than \(\frac{1}{g_m}\). Thus, their parallel combination is dominated by the smaller resistance: \(r_o \parallel \frac{1}{g_m} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}\).
  • The open-circuit small-signal voltage gain (\(A_v\)) of a basic common-emitter amplifier with an effective load resistance \(R_{\text{load}}\) is given by \(A_v = -g_m R_{\text{load}}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, the BJT has a current gain (\(\beta\)) of \(50\). For an emitter-base voltage \(V_{EB} = 600 \text{ mV}\), the emitter-collector voltage \(V_{EC}\) (in Volts) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given, Current gain, \(\beta = 50\) and \(V_{EB} = 600\,\text{mV} = 0.6\,\text{V}\) Given circuit is shown below, Assume transistor is active region : Applying KVL in emitter-base loop (1), \[-3 + V_{EB} + 60\,I_B = 0\] \[3 = V_{EB} + 60\,I_B\] Since, \(V_{EB} = 0.6\,\text{V}\) \[3 - 0.6 = 60\,I_B\] \[I_B = \frac{2.4}{60}\,\text{mA} = 0.04\,\text{mA}\] Applying KVL in emitter collector loop (2), \[-3 + V_{EC} + 0.5\,I_C = 0\] \[3 = V_{EC} + 0.5\,I_C\] \[3 = V_{EC} + 0.5\,\beta I_B \quad [I_C = \beta I_B]\] \[V_{EC} = 3 - 0.5 \times 50 \times 0.04 = 2\,\text{Volts}\] \[V_{EC} > V_{EC(sat)}\] Since, transistor is operate in active region, hence our assumption is correct. Hence, the emitter-collector voltage \(V_{EC}\) is \({2}\,\text{V}\). \[\boxed{V_{EC}=2\text{ V}}\]
Key points
  • When analyzing DC biasing, the standard approach is to assume the transistor is in the active region, calculate the currents using KVL, and then verify the assumption by checking if the junction voltages satisfy the active region conditions (e.g., \(V_{EC} > V_{EC(sat)}\)).
  • Using resistance in \(\text{k}\Omega\) and current in \(\text{mA}\) within KVL equations directly yields the voltage drop in Volts.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An npn BJT having reverse saturation current \(I_S = 10^{-15} \text{ A}\) is biased in the forward active region with \(V_{BE} = 700 \text{ mV}\). The thermal voltage (\(V_T\)) is \(25 \text{ mV}\) and the current gain (\(\beta\)) may vary from 50 to 150 due to manufacturing variations. The maximum emitter current (in \(\mu\text{A}\)) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given \(I_S = 10^{-15}\,\text{A}\), \(V_T = 25\,\text{mV}\) and \(V_{BE} = 700\,\text{mV}\). We know, \[I_C = I_s e^{\frac{V_{BE}}{V_T}} \quad \dots(1)\] \[I_C = 10^{-15} \times e^{(700/25)}\,\text{A}\] \[I_E = \left(1 + \frac{1}{\beta}\right)I_C\] \(I_E\) will be maximum when \(\beta\) is minimum. So when \(\beta = 50\), \[(I_E)_{max} = \left(1 + \frac{1}{50}\right) \times I_C\] \[= 1475 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{A} = {1475}\,\mu\text{A}\] \[\boxed{(I_E)_{max}=1475\mu\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship between collector current and base-emitter voltage is governed by the Ebers-Moll equation: \(I_C = I_S e^{\frac{V_{BE}}{V_T}}\).
  • The emitter current \(I_E\) is the sum of collector current and base current, relating to \(I_C\) via \(I_E = \frac{\beta + 1}{\beta} I_C = \left(1 + \frac{1}{\beta}\right) I_C\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: All the logic gates shown in the figure have a propagation delay of \(20\text{ ns}\). Let \(\text{A} = \text{C} = 0\) and \(\text{B} = 1\) until time \(\text{t} = 0\). At \(\text{t} = 0\), all the inputs flip (i.e., \(\text{A} = \text{C} = 1\) and \(\text{B} = 0\)) and remain in that state. For \(\text{t} > 0\), output \(\text{Z} = 1\) for a duration (in ns) of .
questions.explanation:
The logic circuit has intermediate expressions \(X = \overline{B}\), \(Y = A \cdot X\), and \(Z = Y \oplus C\). Each gate has a propagation delay of \(20\,\text{ns}\). Analyzing the transitions following the input change at \(t = 0\):
  • \(0 \le t < 20\,\text{ns}\): Signals hold initial states because of the propagation delays of gates: \(X = 0\), \(Y = 0\), \(Z = 0\).
  • \(20\,\text{ns} \le t < 40\,\text{ns}\): \(X\) becomes \(\overline{0} = 1\). \(Y\) stays \(1 \cdot 0 = 0\). \(Z\) updates to \(0 \oplus 1 = 1\).
  • \(40\,\text{ns} \le t < 60\,\text{ns}\): \(Y\) updates to \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\). \(Z\) holds its state: \(0 \oplus 1 = 1\).
  • \(t \ge 60\,\text{ns}\): \(Z\) responds to the updated \(Y\): \(1 \oplus 1 = 0\).
The output remains \(Z = 1\) from \(20\,\text{ns}\) to \(60\,\text{ns}\). \[\Delta t = 60\,\text{ns} - 20\,\text{ns} = 40\,\text{ns}\] \[\boxed{40}\]
Key points
  • The phenomena occured above is called a glitch. A Glitch is a temporary, unwanted switching transient at the output before the circuit settles to its steady-state value.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q2
questions.question: A 3-input majority gate is defined by the logic function \(M(a,b,c) = ab + bc + ca\). Which one of the following gates is represented by the function \(M(\overline{M(a,b,c)}, M(a,b,\overline{c}), c)\) ?
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given: \(M(a, b, c) = ab + bc + ca\) \[\begin{aligned} \overline{M(a, b, c)} &= \overline{(ab + bc + ca)} \\ M(a, b, \bar{c}) &= ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a \end{aligned}\] Then, \(M\left[\overline{M(a, b, c)}, M(a, b, \bar{c}), c\right] =\) \[\begin{aligned} & \overline{(ab + bc + ca)}(ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a) \\ & +(ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a)c + c(ab + bc + ca) \\ = & \left[(\overline{ab}\,\overline{bc}\,\overline{ca})\right](ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a) \\ & +(ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a)c + \left[(\overline{ab}\,\overline{bc}\,\overline{ca})\right]c \\ = & \left[(\bar{a} + \bar{b})(\bar{b} + \bar{c})(\bar{c} + \bar{a})\right](ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a) \\ & +abc + (\bar{a} + \bar{b})(\bar{b} + \bar{c})(\bar{c} + \bar{a})c \\ = & (\bar{a} + \bar{b})(\bar{b} + \bar{c})(\bar{c} + \bar{a})\left[ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a + c\right] + abc \end{aligned}\] Since, \(x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)\) \[\begin{aligned} &= (\bar{a} + \bar{b})(\bar{b} + \bar{c})(\bar{c} + \bar{a})(a + b + c) + abc \\ &= (\bar{a}\bar{b} + \bar{b}\bar{c} + \bar{c}\bar{a})(a + b + c) + abc \\ &= a\bar{b}\bar{c} + b\bar{c}\bar{a} + c\bar{a}\bar{b} + abc \\ &= (a\bar{b} + \bar{a}b)\bar{c} + c(\bar{a}\bar{b} + ab) \\ &= (a \oplus b)\bar{c} + (\overline{a \oplus b})c \\ F &= a \oplus b \oplus c \end{aligned}\]
Method 2
(i) \(M(a, b, c) = ab + bc + ca\) K-map for \(M(a, b, c)\) is shown below, \(M(a, b, c) = \Sigma m(3, 5, 6, 7)\) Hence, \(\overline{M(a, b, c)} = \overline{\Sigma m(3, 5, 6, 7)} = \Sigma m(0, 1, 2, 4)\) (ii) \(M(a, b, \bar{c}) = ab + b\bar{c} + \bar{c}a\) K-map for \(M(a, b, \bar{c})\) is shown below, \(M(a, b, \bar{c}) = \Sigma m(2, 4, 6, 7)\) (iii) \(M(c) = c\) K-map is shown below, \(= \Sigma m(1, 3, 5, 7)\) \[\begin{aligned} & M\left[\overline{M(a, b, c)}, M(a, b, \bar{c}), c\right] \\ &= \overline{M(a, b, c)}M(a, b, \bar{c}) + M(a, b, \bar{c})c + \overline{M(a, b, c)}c \\ &= \Sigma m(0, 1, 2, 4)\Sigma m(2, 4, 6, 7) + \Sigma m(2, 4, 6, 7)\Sigma m(1, 3, 5, 7) \\ & \quad + \Sigma m(1, 3, 5, 7)\Sigma m(0, 1, 2, 4) \\ &= \Sigma m(2, 4) + \Sigma m(7) + \Sigma m(1) \\ &= \Sigma m(1, 2, 4, 7) \end{aligned}\] \[\begin{aligned} M\left[\overline{M(a, b, c)}, M(a, b, \bar{c}), c\right] &= \bar{a}\bar{b}c + \bar{a}b\bar{c} + a\bar{b}\bar{c} + abc \\ &= (\bar{a}b + a\bar{b})\bar{c} + (ab + \bar{a}\bar{b})c \\ &= (a \oplus b)\bar{c} + (\overline{a \oplus b})c \\ &= a \oplus b \oplus c \end{aligned}\]
(B) 3-input XOR gate
(NOTE: The IIT official answer key gives only XOR Gate as the correct answer but since a 3 input XOR gate is equivalent to a 3 input X NOR gate option (D) should also be correct.)

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q3
questions.question: A universal logic gate can implement any Boolean function by connecting sufficient number of them appropriately. Three gates are shown. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: None of the gates shown is a universal gate.
questions.explanation:
Method 1
A logic gate is considered universal if it can implement any Boolean function, which means it must be able to replicate the three basic operations: NOT, OR, and AND.
  • NOT operation using Gate 3:
    By fixing the input \(Y = 0\): \[F_3 = \bar{X} + Y = \bar{X} + 0 = \bar{X}\]
  • OR operation using Gate 3:
    By cascading two gates where the first acts as a NOT gate for input \(X\): \[F_3(\bar{X}, Y) = \overline{(\bar{X})} + Y = X + Y\]
  • AND operation using Gate 3:
    By applying De Morgan's Law using three gates: \[F_3(Y, 0) = \bar{Y}\] \[F_3(X, 0) = \bar{X}\] Applying these to another gate with a fixed \(0\) input creates the complement of their sum: \[\overline{(\bar{X} + \bar{Y})} = X \cdot Y\]
Since all basic operations can be implemented, Gate 3 is a universal gate.
Method 2
A functional completeness check requires a gate to possess both a non-linear functionality (like AND/OR) and an inverting functionality (NOT).
  • Gate 1 (\(X + Y\)) and Gate 2 (\(X \cdot Y\)) lack any inverting mechanism, so they cannot produce a NOT operation.
  • Gate 3 (\(\bar{X} + Y\)) contains an internal inverter on input \(X\), allowing it to generate the inversion needed for universal implementation.
\[\boxed{\text{(C) Gate 3 is a universal gate.}}\]
Key points
  • A set of gates is universal if it can implement NOT, AND, and OR functions.
  • An inhibition gate like \(F = \bar{X}Y\) or \(F = \bar{X}+Y\) is functionally complete when fixed logic levels (\(0\) or \(1\)) are available.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume only NAND and NOR can be universal; any gate that can independently implement NOT and either AND/OR with appropriate constant inputs is universal.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q4
questions.question: In the figure shown, the output \(Y\) is required to be \(Y = A B + \overline{C}\,\overline{D}\). The gates G1 and G2 must be, respectively,
questions.explanation:
The target output expression is given as: \[Y = AB + \bar{C}\bar{D}\] Let the output of gate \(G_1\) be \(M\), and the output of the bottom NOR gate be \(N\).
  • Analysis of the bottom branch:
    The inputs \(C\) and \(D\) pass through a standard NOR gate: \[N = \overline{C + D} = \bar{C}\bar{D}\]
  • Analysis of gate \(G_2\):
    The total output \(Y\) is the combination of \(M\) and \(N\) via gate \(G_2\): \[Y = M + N = M + \bar{C}\bar{D}\] Comparing this with the target expression \(Y = AB + \bar{C}\bar{D}\), we can deduce that \(G_2\) must perform an OR operation, and the output from \(G_1\) must be: \[M = AB\]
  • Analysis of gate \(G_1\):
    The inputs entering \(G_1\) are \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{B}\). We need the output to be \(M = AB\). Using De Morgan's Law: \[M = AB = \overline{\bar{A} + \bar{B}}\] This matches the exact functional description of a NOR gate processing \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{B}\).
Thus, \(G_1\) is a NOR gate and \(G_2\) is an OR gate. \[\boxed{\text{(A) NOR, OR}}\]
Key points
  • According to De Morgan's Laws: \(\overline{A+B} = \bar{A}\cdot\bar{B}\) and \(\overline{A\cdot B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}\).
  • An OR gate with inverted inputs behaves as a NAND gate (bubbled OR is equivalent to NAND).
  • An AND gate with inverted inputs behaves as a NOR gate (bubbled AND is equivalent to NOR).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid mixing up the order of \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) when selecting the option, as "OR, NAND" or alternative configurations are present to cause confusion.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Representation of Boolean Expressions and K-Maps Q1
questions.question: A function of Boolean variables \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) is expressed in terms of the min-terms as \[F(X, Y, Z) = \Sigma\,(1, 2, 5, 6, 7)\] Which one of the product of sums given below is equal to the function \(F(X, Y, Z)\)?
options: \((\overline{X} + \overline{Y} + Z) \cdot (\overline{X} + Y + \overline{Z}) \cdot (X + \overline{Y} + Z) \cdot (X + Y + \overline{Z}) \cdot (X + Y + Z)\)
questions.explanation:
The given function is expressed in sum-of-products (SOP) form using minterms: \[F(X, Y, Z) = \sum m(1, 2, 5, 6, 7)\] To convert it into the product-of-sums (POS) form, we find the remaining maxterms that are not present in the minterm list: \[F(X, Y, Z) = \prod M(0, 3, 4)\] Converting each numeric maxterm index into its corresponding binary and algebraic form:
  • \(M_0 = 000_2 \implies (X + Y + Z)\)
  • \(M_3 = 011_2 \implies (X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z})\)
  • \(M_4 = 100_2 \implies (\overline{X} + Y + Z)\)
Multiplying these individual maxterms gives the complete POS expression: \[F(X, Y, Z) = (X + Y + Z) \cdot (X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z}) \cdot (\overline{X} + Y + Z)\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) } (X + Y + Z) \cdot (X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z}) \cdot (\overline{X} + Y + Z)}\]
Key points
  • Minterms and Maxterms are complementary sets for any given Boolean function: \(F = \sum m_i = \prod M_j\), where \(i \notin j\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid treating a maxterm expression as simply the literal-by-literal complemented version of a minterm expression. Remember their fundamental definitions:
    • SOP (Minterms) maps an input bit of \(1\) to (\(A\)) and \(0\) to (\(\overline{A}\)).
    • POS (Maxterms) maps an input bit of \(0\) to (\(A\)) and \(1\) to (\(\overline{A}\)).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Representation of Boolean Expressions and K-Maps Q2
questions.question: The Boolean expression \(\text{F}(\text{X},\text{Y},\text{Z}) = \overline{\text{X}}\,\text{Y}\,\overline{\text{Z}} + \text{X}\,\overline{\text{Y}}\,\overline{\text{Z}} + \text{X}\,\text{Y}\,\overline{\text{Z}} + \text{X}\,\text{Y}\,\text{Z}\) converted into the canonical product of sum (POS) form is
questions.explanation:
The given canonical sum-of-products (SOP) expression is: \[F(X, Y, Z) = \overline{X}Y\overline{Z} + X\overline{Y}\,\overline{Z} + XY\overline{Z} + XYZ\] Identifying the minterms by converting each product term to its binary equivalent (\(1\) for uncomplemented, \(0\) for complemented):
  • \(\overline{X}Y\overline{Z} \implies 010_2 = m_2\)
  • \(X\overline{Y}\,\overline{Z} \implies 100_2 = m_4\)
  • \(XY\overline{Z} \implies 110_2 = m_6\)
  • \(XYZ \implies 111_2 = m_7\)
Thus, \(F(X,Y,Z) = \sum m(2, 4, 6, 7)\). The canonical product-of-sums (POS) form consists of the remaining maxterms not present in the minterm list: \[F(X, Y, Z) = \prod M(0, 1, 3, 5)\] Converting these maxterm indices back to algebraic form (\(0\) for uncomplemented, \(1\) for complemented):
  • \(M_0 = 000_2 \implies (X + Y + Z)\)
  • \(M_1 = 001_2 \implies (X + Y + \overline{Z})\)
  • \(M_3 = 011_2 \implies (X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z})\)
  • \(M_5 = 101_2 \implies (\overline{X} + Y + \overline{Z})\)
Multiplying the maxterms yields: \[F(X, Y, Z) = (X + Y + Z)(X + Y + \overline{Z})(X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z})(\overline{X} + Y + \overline{Z})\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) } (X + Y + Z)(X + Y + \overline{Z})(X + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z})(\overline{X} + Y + \overline{Z})}\]
Key points
  • A Boolean function can be uniquely defined by either its minterm list (\(\sum m\)) or its maxterm list (\(\prod M\)).
  • The total number of minterms and maxterms for an \(n\)-variable function equals \(2^n\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid the common misconception that the POS form is simply the complemented version of the SOP form (or vice versa). They are actually two distinct, independent structural representations of the same underlying Boolean function (\(F\)).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A 1-to-8 demultiplexer with data input \(\text{D}_{\text{in}}\), address inputs \(\text{S}_0\), \(\text{S}_1\), \(\text{S}_2\) (with \(\text{S}_0\) as the LSB) and \(\overline{\text{Y}}_0\) to \(\overline{\text{Y}}_7\) as the eight demultiplexed outputs, is to be designed using two 2-to-4 decoders (with enable input \(\overline{E}\) and address inputs \(\text{A}_0\) and \(\text{A}_1\)) as shown in the figure. \(\text{D}_{\text{in}}\), \(\text{S}_0\), \(\text{S}_1\) and \(\text{S}_2\) are to be connected to P, Q, R and S, but not necessarily in this order. The respective input connections to P, Q, R, and S terminals should beS
questions.explanation:
Consider a \(1 \times 8\) demultiplexer layout: The functional output expressions for this \(1 \times 8\) DE-MUX are defined as follows:
\(\overline{Y}_0 = \overline{\overline{S}_2\,\overline{S}_1\,\overline{S}_0 D_{in}} = \overline{D}_{in} + S_2 + S_1 + S_0\)\(\overline{Y}_4 = \overline{S}_2\,\overline{S}_1\,\overline{S}_0 D_{in} = \overline{D}_{in} + \overline{S}_2 + S_1 + S_0\)
\(\overline{Y}_1 = \overline{\overline{S}_2\,\overline{S}_1 S_0 D_{in}} = \overline{D}_{in} + S_2 + S_1 + \overline{S}_0\)\(\overline{Y}_5 = \overline{S}_2\,\overline{S}_1 S_0 D_{in} = \overline{D}_{in} + \overline{S}_2 + S_1 + \overline{S}_0\)
\(\overline{Y}_2 = \overline{\overline{S}_2 S_1\,\overline{S}_0 D_{in}} = \overline{D}_{in} + S_2 + \overline{S}_1 + S_0\)\(\overline{Y}_6 = \overline{S}_2 S_1\,\overline{S}_0 D_{in} = \overline{D}_{in} + \overline{S}_2 + \overline{S}_1 + S_0\)
\(\overline{Y}_3 = \overline{\overline{S}_2 S_1 S_0 D_{in}} = \overline{D}_{in} + S_2 + \overline{S}_1 + \overline{S}_0\)\(\overline{Y}_7 = \overline{S}_2 S_1 S_0 D_{in} = \overline{D}_{in} + \overline{S}_2 + \overline{S}_1 + \overline{S}_0\)
Now, analyzing the given combinational decoder circuit: From the network configuration, the individual output line equations are derived as: \[\overline{Y}_0 = \overline{\overline{1A}_1\,\overline{1A}_0\,\overline{(P + Q)}} = 1A_1 + 1A_0 + P + Q = S + R + P + Q\] \[\overline{Y}_1 = \overline{\overline{1A}_1 1A_0\,\overline{(P + Q)}} = 1A_1 + \overline{1A}_0 + P + Q = S + \overline{R} + P + Q\] \[\overline{Y}_2 = \overline{1A_1\,\overline{1A}_0\,\overline{(P + Q)}} = \overline{1A}_1 + 1A_0 + P + Q = \overline{S} + R + P + Q\] \[\overline{Y}_3 = \overline{1A_1 1A_0\,\overline{(P + Q)}} = \overline{1A}_1 + \overline{1A}_0 + P + Q = \overline{S} + \overline{R} + P + Q\] \[\overline{Y}_4 = \overline{\overline{2A}_1\,\overline{2A}_0\,\overline{(P + \overline{Q})}} = 2A_1 + 2A_0 + P + \overline{Q} = S + R + P + \overline{Q}\] \[\overline{Y}_5 = \overline{\overline{2A}_1 2A_0\,\overline{(P + \overline{Q})}} = 2A_1 + \overline{2A}_0 + P + \overline{Q} = S + \overline{R} + P + \overline{Q}\] \[\overline{Y}_6 = \overline{2A_1\,\overline{2A}_0\,\overline{(P + \overline{Q})}} = \overline{2A}_1 + 2A_0 + P + \overline{Q} = \overline{S} + R + P + \overline{Q}\] \[\overline{Y}_7 = \overline{2A_1 2A_0\,\overline{(P + \overline{Q})}} = \overline{2A}_1 + \overline{2A}_0 + P + \overline{Q} = \overline{S} + \overline{R} + P + \overline{Q}\] By structural comparison of the corresponding terms:
  • Comparing \(\overline{Y}_0\) and \(\overline{Y}_1\): The variation occurs in \(S_0\) only which can be seen same way in \(R \implies R \rightarrow S_0\)
  • Comparing \(\overline{Y}_0\) and \(\overline{Y}_4\): The variation occurs in \(S_2\) only which can be seen same way in \(Q \implies Q \rightarrow S_2\)
  • Comparing \(\overline{Y}_4\) and \(\overline{Y}_6\): The variation occurs in \(S_1\) only which can be seen same way in \(S \implies S \rightarrow S_1\)
  • Establishing that terminal \(P\) drives the inverted data entry node: \(\implies P \rightarrow \overline{D}_{in}\)
The complete equivalent block mapping configuration is illustrated below: \[\boxed{\text{(D) } D_{in}, S_2, S_0, S_1}\]
Key points
  • Demultiplexer line identification is performed by isolating which select bit causes a state inversion between specific pairs of output equations.
  • Cascaded decoder implementations rely on mapping logic functions to separate enable inputs (\(\overline{1E}, \overline{2E}\)) for block selection.

questions.question: The circuit shown consists of J-K flip-flops, each with an active low asynchronous reset (\(\overline{\text{R}}_{\text{d}}\) input). The counter corresponding to this circuit is
questions.explanation:
To determine the type of counter corresponding to the given circuit, we analyze the clock triggering mechanism and the reset logic condition.
  1. Counting Direction (Up or Down Counter)
    • All flip-flops are negative-edge triggered.
    • The clock input of the next stage is driven by the true output \(Q\) of the preceding stage (\(Q_{0}\) drives the clock of \(FF_{1}\), and \(Q_{1}\) drives the clock of \(FF_{2}\)).
    • The transitions can be seen as follows
    • Since the counter advances in increasing binary sequence (\(000 \to 001 \to 010 \to \dots\)), it operates as a binary up counter.
  2. Modulus of the Counter The flip-flops have an active-low asynchronous reset input (\(\overline{R_d}\)). The reset signal is driven by the output of a NAND gate: \[\text{Reset} = \overline{Q_{2}Q_{0}}\] As soon as the counter reaches the state \(Q_{2}Q_{1}Q_{0} = 101\), the NAND gate output becomes: \[\text{Reset} = \overline{1 \cdot 1} = 0\] This active-low signal instantly resets all flip-flops back to \(000\).
Therefore, the state \(101\) (decimal \(5\)) is a transient state and is not counted.The stable states are \(0, 1, 2, 3,\) and \(4\). Since there are \(5\) stable states, it is a (MOD-5) counter. \[\boxed{\text{(A) a modulo-5 binary up counter}}\]
Key points
1.3
Clock Trigger TypeOutput Driving Next StageCounting Direction
Negative-Edge (\(\text{-ve}\))\(Q\)Up Counter
Negative-Edge (\(\text{-ve}\))\(\overline{Q}\)Down Counter
Positive-Edge (\(\text{+ve}\))\(Q\)Down Counter
Positive-Edge (\(\text{+ve}\))\(\overline{Q}\)Up Counter
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not count the reset state (\(101\)) as a valid stable state. The counter only stays in \(101\) for a propagation delay duration(here zero) before resetting to \(000\).

questions.question: A mod-\(n\) counter using a synchronous binary up-counter with synchronous clear input is shown in the figure. The value of \(n\) is .
questions.explanation:
The given circuit features a 4-bit binary up-counter connected to an active-low clear input (\(\overline{\text{CLEAR}}\)). We analyze how the clear condition behaves under synchronous operation.
  1. NAND Gate Condition:
    The active-low clear signal is generated when \(Q_{C} = 1\) and \(Q_{B} = 1\), which first occurs at the count state: \[Q_{D}Q_{C}Q_{B}Q_{A} = 0110_2 = 6_{10}\]
  2. Effect of Synchronous Clear:
    Due to the synchronous clear input, the counter resets to \(0000\) on the next clock edge after reaching state \(6\), resulting in a stable counting sequence from \(0\) to \(6\).
The total number of stable unique states is \(7\). Thus, it is a mod-7 counter (\(n = 7\)). \[\boxed{7}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Consider a four bit D to A converter. The analog value corresponding to digital signals of values 0000 and 0001 are \(0\text{ V}\) and \(0.0625\text{ V}\) respectively. The analog value (in Volts) corresponding to the digital signal 1111 is .
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The step size is the output change for a \(1\text{ LSB}\) increment (\(0001_2\)). Given:
  • \(V_{\text{out}}(0000_2) = 0\text{ V}\)
  • \(V_{\text{out}}(0001_2) = 0.0625\text{ V}\)
  • To find: \(V_{out}\) for \(1111_2\) that is full scale voltage \(V_{FSO}\)
\[\text{Step Size} = 0.0625\text{ V}\] For an \(n\)-bit converter, the total number of non-zero intervals is \(2^n - 1\). For \(n = 4\): \[\text{Total Steps} = 2^4 - 1 = 15\] The Full-Scale Output (\(V_{\text{FSO}}\)) for the input \(1111_2\) is: \[V_{\text{FSO}} = \text{Total Steps} \times \text{Step Size} = 15 \times 0.0625\text{ V} = 0.9375\text{ V}\]
Method 2
The resolution is determined by the variation between consecutive digital codes: \[\text{Step Size} = V_{\text{out}}(0001_2) - V_{\text{out}}(0000_2) = 0.0625\text{ V}\] The voltage output \(V_o\) scales linearly with the decimal equivalent of the binary value: \[(1111)_2 = 2^3 + 2^2 + 2^1 + 2^0 = 15\] \[V_o = 0.0625\text{ V} \times 15 = 0.9375\text{ V}\]
\[\boxed{0.9375}\]
Key points
  • Resolution: The smallest analog increment produced by an LSB change.
  • DAC Transfer Function: \(V_{\text{out}} = \text{Decimal Equivalent} \times \text{Step Size}\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q1
questions.question: An SR latch is implemented using TTL gates as shown in the figure. The set and reset pulse inputs are provided using the push-button switches. It is observed that the circuit fails to work as desired. The SR latch can be made functional by changing
options: NOR gates to NAND gates and inverters to buffers
questions.explanation:
Analyzing the input characteristics of the TTL family:
  • When a switch is unpressed, the inverter input is left floating.
  • In TTL, a floating input naturally acts as a Logic 1.
  • With a floating input of 1, the inverter outputs a 0 to the NOR latch.
  • When a switch is pressed, the input connects to \(5\text{ V}\) (Logic 1). The inverter still outputs a 0.
Because both states supply a static \((0,0)\) input condition to the NOR latch, it remains stuck. Changing the \(5\text{ V}\) connection to Ground resolves this:
  • unpressed floats to logic 1 (inverter outputs 0)
  • pressed pulls down to logic 0 (inverter outputs 1).
Enabling proper latch operation. \[\boxed{\text{(D) } 5\text{ V to ground}}\]
Key points
  • TTL Floating Inputs: Open inputs in standard TTL circuits are treated as logical high level (Logic 1).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q2
questions.question: A \(16\text{ Kb}\) (\(=16,384\text{ bit}\)) memory array is designed as a square with an aspect ratio of one (number of rows is equal to the number of columns). The minimum number of address lines needed for the row decoder is .
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Total capacity of the memory array = \(16\,\text{Kb} = 16,384\,\text{bits}\)
  • Aspect ratio = \(1\) (The number of rows equals the number of columns)
Let the number of rows be \(R\) and the number of columns be \(C\). Since it is a square array: \[R = C\] The total capacity is the product of the number of rows and columns: \[R \times C = 16,384\] \[R^2 = 16,384\] \[R = \sqrt{16,384} = 128\] The number of address lines \(n\) needed for the row decoder to select one of the \(R\) rows satisfies: \[2^n = R\] \[2^n = 128\] \[n = 7\] \[\boxed{7}\]
Key points
  • For a square memory configuration, \(\text{Rows} = \text{Columns} = \sqrt{\text{Total Capacity in bits}}\).
  • A decoder with \(n\) input address lines can uniquely decode \(2^n\) distinct addresses.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q3
questions.question: In the circuit shown, diodes \(\text{D}_1\), \(\text{D}_2\) and \(\text{D}_3\) are ideal, and the inputs \(\text{E}_1\), \(\text{E}_2\) and \(\text{E}_3\) are ``\(0\text{ V}\)'' for logic `0' and ``\(10\text{ V}\)'' for logic `1'. What logic gate does the circuit represent?
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given that logic-\(0 \rightarrow 0\,\text{V}\) and logic-\(1 \rightarrow 10\,\text{V}\). The diodes are ideal.
  • Case 1: If any of the inputs (\(E_1, E_2, E_3\)) is at logic-\(0\) (\(0\,\text{V}\)), the corresponding ideal diode becomes forward-biased and conducts. This pulls the output voltage \(V_0\) down to \(0\,\text{V}\) (logic-\(0\)).
  • Case 2: If all inputs are at logic-\(1\) (\(10\,\text{V}\)), none of the diodes can conduct because there is no potential difference across them to forward-bias them. Thus, no current flows through the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor, and the output voltage \(V_0\) is pulled up to \(10\,\text{V}\) (logic-\(1\)).
The truth table for the operation is:
\(E_1\)\(E_2\)\(E_3\)\(D_1\)\(D_2\)\(D_3\)\(V_0\)
000ONONON0
001ONONOFF0
010ONOFFON0
011ONOFFOFF0
100OFFONON0
101OFFONOFF0
110OFFOFFON0
111OFFOFFOFF1
The output expression is: \[V_0 = E_1 \cdot E_2 \cdot E_3\] Hence, the circuit represents a 3-input AND gate.
Method 2
The given circuit configuration can be identified directly via diode logic analysis:
  • The cathodes of the diodes are connected to the input nodes, and their anodes are tied together at a common interconnecting output node.
  • This common node is connected to a positive supply voltage (\(10\,\text{V}\)) via a pull-up resistor.
  • Such a topology constitutes a standard Wired-AND or Implied AND logic structure.
Therefore, the circuit performs a 3-input AND operation: \[V_0 = E_1 \cdot E_2 \cdot E_3\]
\[\boxed{\text{(C) 3-input AND gate}}\]
Key points
  • A common interconnecting node with a pull-up resistor forms a Wired-AND logic structure.
  • Conversely, a common interconnecting node with a pull-down resistor forms a Wired-OR logic structure.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In an 8085 microprocessor, the shift registers which store the result of an addition and the overflow bit are, respectively
questions.explanation:
To determine which registers store the result of an arithmetic operation and its associated status flags in an 8085 microprocessor, let us look at the architecture of its Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU):
  • Accumulator (Register A):
    • The accumulator is an 8-bit register that is part of the ALU.
    • It is used to store 8-bit data and is always one of the default operands for any multi-operand arithmetic or logical instruction (such as addition or subtraction).
    • Crucially, after the ALU processes the operation, the final result is automatically routed and saved back into the Accumulator (A).
  • Flag Register (Register F):
    • The flag register is an 8-bit status register containing 5 active flip-flops acting as conditional flags.
    • These flags reflect the status conditions of the most recent data result generated by the ALU.
    • Any overflow bit resulting from an arithmetic addition sets or resets the Carry Flag (\(\text{CY}\)) located inside this Flag Register (F).
Therefore, the registers that store the result of an addition and the overflow status bit are A and F, respectively. \[\boxed{\text{(B) A and F}}\]
Key points
  • 8085 Flag Register Layout: The 5 flags inside the 8-bit flag register (F) are structured as: \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline D_7 & D_6 & D_5 & D_4 & D_3 & D_2 & D_1 & D_0 \\ \hline \text{S} & \text{Z} & \times & \text{AC} & \times & \text{P} & \times & \text{CY} \\ \hline \end{array}\] Where \(\text{S} = \text{Sign Flag}\), \(\text{Z} = \text{Zero Flag}\), \(\text{AC} = \text{Auxiliary Carry Flag}\), \(\text{P} = \text{Parity Flag}\), and \(\text{CY} = \text{Carry Flag}\) (which tracks the final overflow/carry bit out of \(D_7\)).
  • Implicit Register Usage: In instructions like ADD B, the operation performed is implicitly \(A \leftarrow A + B\), showing that the accumulator serves as both an input operand source and the destination repository for the output.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In an 8085 microprocessor, which one of the following instructions changes the content of the accumulator?
questions.explanation:
To determine which instruction changes the contents of the accumulator, let us analyze the functionality of each given 8085 instruction:
  • A. MOV B, M:
    This instruction moves an 8-bit data byte from the memory location pointed to by the \(\text{HL}\) register pair into register \(\text{B}\). The contents of the accumulator are completely unaffected.
  • B. PCHL:
    This instruction copies the contents of the \(\text{HL}\) register pair into the Program Counter (\(\text{PC}\)). Specifically, \(\text{PC}_{\text{H}} \leftarrow \text{H}\) and \(\text{PC}_{\text{L}} \leftarrow \text{L}\). It alters the program execution flow but does not modify the accumulator.
  • C. RNZ:
    This is a conditional control transfer instruction (Return if No Zero). It checks the status of the Zero Flag (\(\text{Z}\)). If \(\text{Z} = 0\), the program pops the return address from the stack into the Program Counter (\(\text{PC}\)). This instruction changes only the execution path and does not impact the accumulator data.
  • D. SBI BEH:
    This instruction stands for Subtract Immediate from Accumulator with Borrow. It performs an arithmetic operation on the accumulator register: \[A \leftarrow A - \text{BEH} - \text{CY}\] Since the result of this subtraction is automatically updated and stored back in the accumulator, it directly changes the contents of the accumulator.
\[\boxed{\text{(D) SBI BEH}}\]
Key points
  • Accumulator-centric Instructions: Almost all immediate arithmetic/logical instructions like ADI, SUI, ANI, XRI, and SBI target the accumulator implicitly as both an operand source and destination.
  • SBI <data> explicitly modifies the accumulator along with the flags (\(\text{S}\), \(\text{Z}\), \(\text{AC}\), \(\text{P}\), \(\text{CY}\)) according to the result of the subtraction operation.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Which one of the following 8085 microprocessor programs correctly calculates the product of two 8-bit numbers stored in registers B and C?
questions.explanation:
The problem requires multiplying two 8-bit numbers stored in registers B and C using the successive addition method. In this method, the content of register C is added to the accumulator repeatedly, while register B acts as a down-counter to track the number of additions remaining.
  • Analysis of Option A:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{MVI A, 00H} && \text{; Load immediate value } 00\text{H} \text{ into the Accumulator } (A = 00\text{H}) \\ &\text{JNZ LOOP} && \text{; Jump to LOOP if Zero flag } Z = 0 \text{ (Unpredictable behavior as flags are not yet initialized)} \\ &\text{CMP C} && \text{; Compare Accumulator with Register C} \\ \text{LOOP:\ } &\text{DCR B} && \text{; Decrement Register B by 1 } (B = B - 1) \\ &\text{HLT} && \text{; Halt the processor execution} \end{aligned}\] Explanation: This program contains a conditional jump before any arithmetic operations affect the status flags, lacks an addition step, and directly halts on the first iteration sequence.
  • Analysis of Option B:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{MVI A, 00H} && \text{; Initialize the Accumulator with value } 00\text{H} \\ &\text{CMP C} && \text{; Compare Accumulator with Register C (Updates flags based on } A - C\text{)} \\ \text{LOOP:\ } &\text{DCR B} && \text{; Decrement the loop counter in Register B} \\ &\text{JNZ LOOP} && \text{; Jump back to LOOP if } B \neq 0 \\ &\text{HLT} && \text{; Halt the processor} \end{aligned}\] Explanation: Though the loop structure correctly decrements register B down to zero, the program only performs comparisons (`CMP C`) and completely omits any addition sequence. It does not calculate a product.
  • Analysis of Option C:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{MVI A, 00H} && \text{; Clear Accumulator } (A = 00\text{H}) \text{ to store the running sum} \\ \text{LOOP:\ } &\text{ADD C} && \text{; Accumulator } \leftarrow \text{ Accumulator } + \text{ Register C} \\ &\text{DCR B} && \text{; Decrement Register B by 1. Updates the Zero flag } (Z) \\ &\text{JNZ LOOP} && \text{; If } B \neq 0 \text{ (Zero flag } Z = 0\text{), jump back to LOOP} \\ &\text{HLT} && \text{; Terminate the program when } B = 0 \end{aligned}\] Explanation: This program accurately implements the successive addition algorithm. It initializes the product tracking register (\(A\)) to zero, updates the product with the multiplicand (\(C\)), decrements the multiplier loop counter (\(B\)), and loops continuously until the counter runs down to zero.
  • Analysis of Option D:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{MVI A, 00H} && \text{; Initialize Accumulator } A = 00\text{H} \\ &\text{ADD C} && \text{; Add Register C to Accumulator } (A = A + C) \\ &\text{JNZ LOOP} && \text{; Jump to LOOP if Zero flag } Z = 0 \\ \text{LOOP:\ } &\text{INR B} && \text{; Increment Register B by 1 } (B = B + 1) \\ &\text{HLT} && \text{; Halt the processor} \end{aligned}\] Explanation: This program increments the counter variable (`INR B`) instead of decrementing it towards zero. Furthermore, the `HLT` instruction is positioned immediately following `INR B`, meaning the loop structure terminates prematurely on the first jump execution block.
\[\boxed{\text{(C) } \begin{aligned} &\text{MVI A, 00H} \\ \text{LOOP } &\text{ADD C} \\ &\text{DCR B} \\ &\text{JNZ LOOP} \\ &\text{HLT} \end{aligned}}\]
Key points
  • MVI r, data: Moves an 8-bit immediate value into the designated register \(r\).
  • ADD r: Adds the contents of register \(r\) to the accumulator and stores the result back in the accumulator.
  • DCR r: Decrements the designated register \(r\) by 1. Crucially, it updates the Zero flag based on the result.
  • JNZ label: Jumps to the specified memory location label if the Zero flag is reset (\(Z = 0\)), which corresponds to a non-zero computational result.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Flag dependencies: Always ensure that conditional jump instructions directly follow the specific arithmetic or logical instructions meant to update the control flags.
  • Loop Direction: Confirm that loop counters for deterministic loop executions run toward zero (`DCR`) rather than away from it (`INR`), unless checking for specific overflow boundary conditions.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Negative feedback in a closed loop control system DOES NOT
questions.explanation:
The effects of negative feedback in a closed-loop control system are :
  • Reduction in Overall Gain: The gain of a closed-loop system is \(A_{CL} = \frac{G}{1 + GH}\). Since the denominator \((1 + GH) > 1\), the overall gain is reduced.
  • Increase in Bandwidth: For most systems, the gain-bandwidth product remains constant. Therefore, a decrease in gain results in an increase in bandwidth.
  • Improvement in Disturbance Rejection: Negative feedback reduces the effect of external disturbances and noise signals entering the system thus improving the stability.
  • Reduction in Sensitivity: (\(S^{T}_{G} = \frac{1}{1+GH}\)) It makes the system less sensitive to variations in internal plant parameters \(G\).
\[\text{Gain} \downarrow \implies \text{Bandwidth} \uparrow\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) reduce bandwidth}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q1
questions.question: For the signal flow graph shown in the figure, the value of \(C(s)/R(s)\) is
questions.explanation:
From the given signal flow graph, we can identify the following components:
  • Forward path: \(P_{1} = G_{1} G_{2} G_{3} G_{4}\)
  • Individual loops: \(L_{1} = -G_{1} G_{2} H_{1}, \quad L_{2} = -G_{3} G_{4} H_{2}, \quad L_{3} = -G_{2} G_{3} H_{3}\)
  • Non-touching loops (two at a time): \(L_{1} L_{2} = (-G_{1} G_{2} H_{1})(-G_{3} G_{4} H_{2}) = G_{1} G_{2} H_{1} G_{3} G_{4} H_{2}\)
By applying Mason's Gain Formula: \[\text{TF} = \frac{P_{1}\Delta_{1}}{\Delta} = \frac{G_{1}G_{2}G_{3}G_{4}}{1 - (L_{1} + L_{2} + L_{3}) + (L_{1}L_{2})} = \frac{G_{1}G_{2}G_{3}G_{4}}{1 + G_{1}G_{2}H_{1} + G_{3}G_{4}H_{2} + G_{2}G_{3}H_{3} + G_{1}G_{2}H_{1}G_{3}G_{4}H_{2}}\] \[\boxed{(B) \ \ \frac{G_{1}G_{2}G_{3}G_{4}}{1 + G_{1}G_{2}H_{1} + G_{3}G_{4}H_{2} + G_{2}G_{3}H_{3} + G_{1}G_{2}H_{1}G_{3}G_{4}H_{2}}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Touching vs. Non-touching: Ensure that loops designated as non-touching do not share even a single node.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q2
questions.question: By performing cascading and/or summing/differencing operations using transfer function blocks \(G_1(s)\) and \(G_2(s)\), one CANNOT realize a transfer function of the form
questions.explanation:
Given blocks have transfer functions \(G_{1}(s)\) and \(G_{2}(s)\).
  1. \(G_{1}(s) G_{2}(s) \Rightarrow\) Realization is possible through a cascade connection.
  2. \(\dfrac{G_{1}(s)}{G_{2}(s)} \Rightarrow\) Realization is not possible because division cannot be achieved through cascading, summing, or differencing.
  3. \(G_{1}(s) \left( \dfrac{1}{G_{1}(s)} + G_{2}(s) \right) = 1 + G_{1}(s) G_{2}(s) \Rightarrow\) Realization is possible by summing a unity gain path (identity) with a cascade of \(G_{1}(s)\) and \(G_{2}(s)\).
  4. \(G_{1}(s) \left( \dfrac{1}{G_{1}(s)} - G_{2}(s) \right) = 1 - G_{1}(s) G_{2}(s) \Rightarrow\) Realization is possible by differencing a unity gain path and a cascade of \(G_{1}(s)\) and \(G_{2}(s)\).
\[\boxed{(B) \ \ \dfrac{G_{1}(s)}{G_{2}(s)}}\]
Key points
Algebraic Constraint: Division of transfer functions (\(\frac{G_1}{G_2}\)) requires a feedback configuration or an explicit inverter block, which is not available through simple cascading or summing of \(G_1\) and \(G_2\).

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q3
questions.question: The position control of a DC servo-motor is given in the figure. The values of the parameters are \(K_T = 1 \text{ N-m/A}\), \(R_a = 1 \Omega\), \(L_a = 0.1 \text{H}\), \(J = 5 \text{kg-m}^2\), \(B = 1 \text{ N-m/(rad/sec)}\) and \(K_b = 1 \text{V/(rad/sec)}\). The steady-state position response (in radians) due to unit impulse disturbance torque \(T_d\) is
questions.explanation:
To find the steady-state position response due to the disturbance torque \(T_{d}(s)\), we first determine the transfer function \(\dfrac{\theta(s)}{T_{d}(s)}\) from the given block diagram. Applying the closed-loop transfer function formula: \[\frac{\theta(s)}{T_{d}(s)} = \frac{-\dfrac{1}{s} \left( \dfrac{1}{J s + B} \right)}{1 - \left[ \dfrac{K_{T}}{(R_{a} + L_{a} s)} \dfrac{1}{(J s + B)} K_{b} (-1) \right]} = \frac{-\left( \dfrac{1}{s(J s + B)} \right)}{\dfrac{(R_{a} + L_{a} s)(J s + B) + K_{T} K_{b}}{(R_{a} + L_{a} s)(J s + B)}}\] \[\frac{\theta(s)}{T_{d}(s)} = -\frac{(R_{a} + L_{a} s)}{s [(R_{a} + L_{a} s)(J s + B) + K_{T} K_{b}]}\] For a unit impulse disturbance torque, \(T_{d}(s) = 1\). The output position response is: \[\theta(s) = -\frac{(R_{a} + L_{a} s)}{s [(R_{a} + L_{a} s)(J s + B) + K_{T} K_{b}]}\] Using the Final Value Theorem to find the steady-state position response \(\theta(\infty)\): \[\theta(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \theta(s)\] \[\theta(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{-(R_{a} + L_{a} s)}{s [(R_{a} + L_{a} s)(J s + B) + K_{T} K_{b}]} \right] = \frac{-R_{a}}{(R_{a} B) + K_{T} K_{b}}\] Substituting the given parameter values: \(K_{T} = 1\), \(R_{a} = 1\), \(B = 1\), and \(K_{b} = 1\): \[\theta(\infty) = \frac{-1}{(1)(1) + (1)(1)} = \frac{-1}{2} = -0.5\] \[\boxed{\text{Steady State Position response} = -0.5}\]
Key points
Transfer Function with Disturbance: When finding response to disturbance, treat other inputs (like \(V_{a}(s)\)) as zero.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A unity negative feedback system has an open-loop transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{s(s+10)}\). The gain \(K\) for the system to have a damping ratio of \(0.25\) is
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation for the unity feedback system is: \[1 + G(s) = 0 \implies 1 + \frac{K}{s(s+10)} = 0\] \[s^2 + 10s + K = 0\] Comparing with the standard second-order equation \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\): \[\omega_n^2 = K \implies \omega_n = \sqrt{K}\] \[2\xi\omega_n = 10 \implies \xi\omega_n = 5\] Given the damping ratio \(\xi = 0.25\): \[0.25 \times \sqrt{K} = 5\] \[\sqrt{K} = \frac{5}{0.25} = 20\] \[\boxed{K=400}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The characteristic equation of an LTI system is given by \(F(s) = s^5 + 2s^4 + 3s^3 + 6s^2 - 4s - 8 = 0\). The number of roots that lie strictly in the left half of s-plane is
questions.explanation:
Routh Table Construction:
\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} s^5 & 1 & 3 & -4 \\ s^4 & 2 & 6 & -8 \\ s^3 & 0\,(8) & 0\,(12) & 0 \\ s^2 & 3 & -8 & 0 \\ s^1 & \dfrac{100}{3} & 0 & 0 \\ s^0 & -8 & & \end{array}\] Auxiliary equation from \(s^4\) row: \[A(s) = 2s^4 + 6s^2 - 8 = 0\] Taking derivative with respect to \(s\): \[\frac{dA(s)}{ds} = 8s^3 + 12s = 0\] There is exactly 1 sign change in the first column, which occurs below the row of zeros (\(s^3\)). Analyzing the auxiliary equation \(A(s)\): \[2s^4 + 6s^2 - 8 = 0 \implies s^4 + 3s^2 - 4 = 0\] \[(s^2 + 4)(s^2 - 1) = 0\] The roots of \(A(s)\) are: \[s = \pm 2j, \quad s = \pm 1\]
  • Roots in RHS (\(\text{RHP}\)) \(= 1\) (at \(s = 1\))
  • Roots on \(j\omega\)-axis \(= 2\) (at \(s = \pm 2j\))
  • Total roots \(= 5\)
Roots in LHS (\(\text{LHP}\)) \(= 5 - 1 - 2 = \boxed{2}\).
Key points
If there is a sign change above the row of zeros,non-symmetric roots are there. However, if there is a sign change below the row of zeros, the root lies on the RHP and its symmetric root lies on the LHP.If there is no sign change below ROZ,symmetric poles lie strictly on imaginary axis

questions.question: A unity negative feedback system has the open-loop transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{s(s + 1)(s + 3)}\). The value of the gain \(K(>0)\) at which the root locus crosses the imaginary axis is
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation of the unity negative feedback control system is given by \(1 + G(s) = 0\): \[1 + \frac{K}{s(s + 1)(s + 3)} = 0 \implies s^3 + 4s^2 + 3s + K = 0\] RH Table: \[\begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & 3 \\ s^2 & 4 & K \\ s^1 & \dfrac{12 - K}{4} & 0 \\ s^0 & K \end{array}\] For the system branches to cross the imaginary axis, the system must cross the threshold of marginal stability. Setting the elements of the \(s^1\) row to zero: \[\frac{12 - K}{4} = 0 \implies \boxed{K = 12}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: For the system shown in the figure, \(s = -2.75\) lies on the root locus if \(K\) is
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Angle Condition Check The open-loop transfer function is: \[G(s)H(s) = \frac{10K(s + 3)}{s + 2}\] For \(s = -2.75\) to lie on the root locus, it must satisfy the angle condition: \[\angle G(s)H(s) = \frac{\angle K + \angle(s + 3)}{\angle(s + 2)}\] \[= \angle K + \angle(s + 3) - \angle(s + 2)\] \[= 0^\circ + \angle(-2.75 + 3) - \angle(-2.75 + 2)\] \[= \angle(0.25) - \angle(-0.75)\] \[= 0^\circ - 180^\circ = -180^\circ\] Since the angle is \(-180^\circ\), it satisfies the angle condition \(\pm 180^\circ(2k + 1)\). Thus, the point lies on the root locus. Step 2: Magnitude Condition Since the angle condition is verified, we apply the magnitude criteria to find \(K\): \[|G(s)H(s)|_{s = -2.75} = 1\] \[\left| \frac{10K(s + 3)}{s + 2} \right|_{s = -2.75} = 1\] \[K = \left| \frac{-2.75 + 2}{10(-2.75 + 3)} \right|\] \[K = \frac{0.75}{2.5} = 0.3\] \[\boxed{0.3}\]
Mistakes to avoid
The angle condition must be satisfied first to ensure a point truly lies on the root locus; only then should the magnitude condition be applied to calculate the value of \(K\).

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The open-loop transfer function of a unity feedback configuration is given as, \(G(s) = \dfrac{K(s + 4)}{(s + 8)(s^2 - 9)}\). The value of gain \(K\ (> 0)\) for which \(-1 + j2\) lies on the root locus is
questions.explanation: Given the open-loop transfer function of a unity feedback system (\(H(s) = 1\)): \[G(s) = \frac{K(s+4)}{(s+8)(s^2-9)} = \frac{K(s+4)}{(s+8)(s+3)(s-3)}\] Step 1: Angle Condition Check \[\angle G(s)H(s) = \frac{\angle K + \angle(s+4)}{\angle(s+8) + \angle(s+3) + \angle(s-3)}\] Evaluating at \(s = -1 + j2\): \[= \frac{\angle K + \angle(-1+j2+4)}{\angle(-1+j2+8) + \angle(-1+j2+3) + \angle(-1+j2-3)}\] \[= \frac{0^\circ + \angle(3+j2)}{\angle(7+j2) + \angle(2+j2) + \angle(-4+j2)}\] \[= \frac{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{7}\right) + \tan^{-1}(1) + \left(180^\circ - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)}\] \[= 33.69^\circ - 15.945^\circ - 45^\circ - 180^\circ + 26.565^\circ\] \[= -180.72^\circ \simeq -180^\circ\] Since it satisfies \(\pm 180^\circ(2Q + 1)\), the point lies on the root locus. Step 2: Magnitude Condition Applying magnitude criteria to calculate system gain \(K\): \[|G(s)H(s)|_{s=-1+j2} = 1\] \[\frac{K\sqrt{(-1+4)^2 + 2^2}}{\sqrt{(-1+8)^2 + 2^2}\cdot\sqrt{(-1+3)^2 + 2^2}\cdot\sqrt{(-1-3)^2 + 2^2}} = 1\] \[\frac{K\sqrt{9+4}}{\sqrt{49+4}\cdot\sqrt{4+4}\cdot\sqrt{16+4}} = 1\] \[\frac{K\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{53}\cdot\sqrt{8}\cdot\sqrt{20}} = 1\] \[K = \frac{\sqrt{53 \times 8 \times 20}}{\sqrt{13}} \simeq 25.54\] \[\boxed{25.54}\]

questions.question: The phase margin (in degrees) of the system \(G(s) = \dfrac{10}{s(s+10)}\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given, \[G(s)=\frac{10}{s(s+10)}\] Substituting \(s=j\omega\), \[G(j\omega)=\frac{10}{j\omega(j\omega+10)}\] Magnitude condition at gain cross-over frequency: \[|G(j\omega_{gc})|=1\] \[\left| \frac{10}{j\omega(j\omega+10)} \right| =1\] \[\frac{10}{\omega\sqrt{\omega^{2}+10^{2}}}=1\] \[100=\omega^{2}(\omega^{2}+100)\] \[\omega^{4}+100\omega^{2}-100=0\] \[\text{Let }~ x=\omega^{2}\] \[x^{2}+100x-100=0\] The valid root of the above quadratic expression is: \[x=0.99\] \[\omega_{gc}=\sqrt{0.99}\approx 0.995\,\text{rad/s}\] Phase angle at gain cross-over frequency: \[\angle G(j\omega) = -90^{\circ} -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega}{10}\right)\] At \(\omega=\omega_{gc}\), \[\angle G(j\omega_{gc}) = -90^{\circ} -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{0.995}{10}\right) = -95.68^{\circ}\] Phase margin is \[PM = 180^{\circ} + \angle G(j\omega_{gc}) = 84.32^{\circ}\] \[\boxed{84.32^{\circ}}\]
Key points
  • Gain cross-over frequency is the frequency at which \[|G(j\omega)|=1\]
  • Phase margin is given by \[PM=180^{\circ}+\angle G(j\omega_{gc})\]
  • Pole at origin contributes \(-90^{\circ}\) phase shift.

questions.question:
The transfer function of a mass-spring-damper system is given by \[G(s)=\frac{1}{Ms^2+Bs+K}\] The frequency response data for the system are given in the following table. \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\omega \text{ in rad/s} & |G(j\omega)| \text{ in dB} & \arg(G(j\omega)) \text{ in deg} \\
\hline
0.01 & -18.5 & -0.2 \\
\hline
0.1 & -18.5 & -1.3 \\
\hline
0.2 & -18.4 & -2.6 \\
\hline
1 & -16 & -16.9 \\
\hline
2 & -11.4 & -89.4 \\
\hline
3 & -21.5 & -151 \\
\hline
5 & -32.8 & -167 \\
\hline
10 & -45.3 & -174.5 \\
\hline
\end{array}\] The unit step response of the system approaches a steady state value of .
questions.explanation: For a unit step input, the steady-state value is equal to the DC gain of the system. The DC gain is obtained by putting \(s=0\) in \[G(s)=\frac{1}{Ms^2+Bs+K}.\] Thus, \[G(0)=\frac{1}{K}.\] From the frequency response table, at very low frequency, \(|G(j\omega)|\approx 10^{-18.5/20}\), since the phase is nearly \(0^\circ\). Therefore, \[\frac{1}{K}=10^{-18.5/20}\approx0.1189.\] Hence, the steady-state value of the unit step response is \[\boxed{0.12}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Consider the Bode plot shown in the figure. Assume that all the poles and zeros are real-valued. The value of \(f_H-f_L\) (in Hz) is .
questions.explanation:
The slope of the Bode plot is \(+40\,\text{dB/decade}\) from \(f_L\) to \(300\,\text{Hz}\). Since the magnitude increases by \(40\,\text{dB}\), \[40\log_{10}\left(\frac{300}{f_L}\right)=40\] \[\log_{10}\left(\frac{300}{f_L}\right)=1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{300}{f_L}=10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad f_L=30\,\text{Hz}.\] Similarly, the slope is \(-40\,\text{dB/decade}\) from \(900\,\text{Hz}\) to \(f_H\). Hence, \[40\log_{10}\left(\frac{f_H}{900}\right)=40\] \[\log_{10}\left(\frac{f_H}{900}\right)=1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{f_H}{900}=10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad f_H=9000\,\text{Hz}.\] Therefore, \[f_H-f_L=9000-30=8970\,\text{Hz}.\] \[\boxed{8970\,\text{Hz}}\]
Key points
  • A slope of \(\pm40\,\text{dB/decade}\) means a \(40\,\text{dB}\) change corresponds to one decade, i.e., a frequency ratio of \(10\).
  • Thus, \(f_L=300/10=30\,\text{Hz}\) and \(f_H=900\times10=9000\,\text{Hz}\).

questions.question: The transfer function of a first-order controller is given as \[G_c(s)=\frac{K(s+a)}{s+b}\] where \(K\), \(a\) and \(b\) are positive real numbers. The condition for this controller to act as a phase lead compensator is
questions.explanation:
Given, \[G_c(s)=\frac{K(s+a)}{s+b}\] where \(K\), \(a\) and \(b\) are positive real numbers. Comparing with the standard compensator form, \[G_c(s)=K\frac{s+z}{s+p}\] we get, \[z=a \qquad \text{and} \qquad p=b\] For a phase lead compensator, \[z<p\] because the zero must lie closer to the origin than the pole. Therefore, \(a<b\) \[\boxed{\text{(A) a<b}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not compare the numerical values directly without understanding pole-zero locations on the negative real axis.
  • Remember that the locations are \[s=-a \quad \text{and} \quad s=-b\] not \(+a\) and \(+b\).

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A lead compensator network includes a parallel combination of \(R\) and \(C\) in the feed-forward path. If the transfer function of the compensator is \[G_c(s)=\frac{s+2}{s+4},\] the value of \(RC\) is .
questions.explanation: For a lead compensator, \[G_c(s)=\frac{1+\tau s}{1+\alpha\tau s}\] Given, \[G_c(s)=\frac{s+2}{s+4}\] Rewriting, \[G_c(s)=\frac{1+\dfrac{s}{2}}{1+\dfrac{s}{4}}\] Comparing with the standard form, \[\tau=\frac{1}{2}\] Since \[\tau=RC\] \[RC=\frac{1}{2}\] \[RC=0.5\] \[\boxed{0.5}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A zero mean white Gaussian noise having power spectral density \(\dfrac{N_0}{2}\) is passed through an LTI filter whose impulse response \(h(t)\) is shown in the figure. The variance of the filtered noise at \(t=4\) is
questions.explanation: Theory: Passing a Gaussian random process through an LTI system preserves Gaussianity. Also, for zero-mean WSS noise, variance equals output power. A Gaussian random process \(X(t)\) is passed through an LTI system to produce \(Y(t)\). Sampling a Gaussian random process gives a Gaussian random variable. Hence, \(Y(t_i)\) has Gaussian distribution with mean and variance same as the Gaussian random process \(Y(t)\). The output PSD is \[S_Y(f) = |H(f)|^2S_X(f)\]where \(S_X(f)=\dfrac{N_0}{2}\). The variance is given by \[\text{Variance} = \text{mean square value} - (\text{mean})^2\]The mean of the output process is \[m_Y(t) = H(0)m_X(t)\]Since the input has zero mean, \[m_X(t)=0\]Therefore, \[m_Y(t)=0\]Hence, variance becomes equal to output power. The output power is \[P_Y = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_Y(f)\,df\] \[= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |H(f)|^2\frac{N_0}{2}\,df\] \[= \frac{N_0}{2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^2\,df\]Using Parseval’s theorem, \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^2\,df = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|^2\,dt\]Given, \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|^2\,dt = 3A^2\]Therefore, \[P_Y = \frac{N_0}{2}(3A^2)\] \[= \frac{3}{2}N_0A^2\]Thus, the variance at \(t=4\) or equivalently at \(\tau=0\) is \[\boxed{(A) \sigma_Y^2 = \frac{3}{2}N_0A^2 }\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: \(\{X_n\}_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\) is an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random process with \(X_n\) equally likely to be \(+1\) or \(-1\). \(\{Y_n\}_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\) is another random process obtained as \[Y_n = X_n + 0.5X_{n-1}.\] The autocorrelation function of \(\{Y_n\}_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\), denoted by \(R_Y[k]\), is
questions.explanation: For the discrete random variables \(X_n\), the autocorrelation function is \[R_X(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} [X_nX_{n+k}]_iP_i \tag{1}\]where \(P_i\) is the probability of occurrence of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) symbol. Since \(X_n\) is equally likely to be \(1\) or \(-1\), \[P(1)=P(-1)=\frac12\]For \(k=0\), \[R_X(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{2}(X_nX_n)_iP_i\] \[= (1)(1)\left(\frac12\right) + (-1)(-1)\left(\frac12\right)\] \[= 1\]Hence, \[R_X(k)=1, \qquad k=0\]For \(k\ne0\), there are four possible combinations of \(X_n\) and \(X_{n+k}\). \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline X_n & X_{n+k} & P_i \\ \hline 1 & -1 & 1/4 \\ \hline -1 & 1 & 1/4 \\ \hline -1 & -1 & 1/4 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 1/4 \\ \hline \end{array}\] \[R_X(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{4}(X_nX_{n+k})_iP_i\] \[= (1)(-1)\left(\frac14\right) + (-1)(1)\left(\frac14\right) + (-1)(-1)\left(\frac14\right) + (1)(1)\left(\frac14\right)\] \[= -\frac14-\frac14+\frac14+\frac14\] \[= 0\]Therefore, \[R_X(k)= \begin{cases} 1, & k=0\\ 0, & k\ne0 \end{cases} \tag{2}\] Given, \[Y_n=X_n+0.5X_{n-1}\]The autocorrelation of \(Y_n\) is \[R_Y(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}(Y_nY_{n+k})_iP_i\]Substituting \(Y_n\), \[R_Y(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left[ (X_n+0.5X_{n-1}) (X_{n+k}+0.5X_{n-1+k}) \right]_iP_i\]Expanding, \[R_Y(k) = R_X(k) + 0.5R_X(k-1) + 0.5R_X(k+1) + 0.25R_X(k)\] \[R_Y(k) = 1.25R_X(k) + 0.5R_X(k-1) + 0.5R_X(k+1)\]For \(k=0\), \[R_Y(0) = R_X(0) + 0.5R_X(-1) + 0.5R_X(1) + 0.25R_X(0)\]Using (2), \[R_Y(0) = 1+0+0+0.25\] \[= 1.25\]For \(k=1\), \[R_Y(1) = R_X(1) + 0.5R_X(0) + 0.5R_X(2) + 0.25R_X(1)\] \[= 0+0.5(1)+0+0\] \[= 0.5\]Similarly, \[R_Y(-1)=0.5\]For all other values of \(k\), \[R_Y(k)=0\]Therefore, \[\boxed{ (B) R_Y(k)= \begin{cases} 1.25, & k=0\\ 0.5, & k=\pm1\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} }\]
