questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A random binary wave \(y(t)\) is given by \[y(t)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} X_n\,p(t-nT-\phi)\]where \[p(t)=u(t)-u(t-T),\]\(u(t)\) is the unit step function and \(\phi\) is an independent random variable with uniform distribution in \([0,T]\). The sequence \(\{X_n\}\) consists of independent and identically distributed binary valued random variables with \(P\{X_n=+1\}=P\{X_n=-1\}=0.5\) for each \(n\).The value of the autocorrelation\[R_{yy}\left(\frac{3T}{4}\right)\triangleq E\left[y(t)\,y\left(t-\frac{3T}{4}\right)\right]\]equals .
questions.explanation: Theory: The autocorrelation depends on the overlap between two shifted pulses. Greater overlap gives larger correlation. Given, \[y(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} X_n\,p(t-nT-\phi)\]The autocorrelation function is \[R_{yy}(t_i,t_j) = E[y(t_i)y(t_j)]\] \[= E[X_iX_j]\, p(t_i-nT-\phi)\, p(t_j-nT-\phi)\] (a) If \(\mathbf{|t_i-t_j|>T}\) The pulses are either adjacent or distinct, hence the random variables are uncorrelated. \[E[X_iX_j] = E[X_i]E[X_j]\]Given, \[E[X_n] = 0.5(1)+(-1)(0.5) = 0\]Therefore, \[E[X_iX_j]=0 \tag{1}\] (b) If \(\mathbf{|t_i-t_j|<T}\) The pulses overlap, hence correlation exists. \[E[X_iX_j] = E[X_i^2]\] \[= (1)^2(0.5)+(-1)^2(0.5)\] \[= 1 \tag{2}\] The random variable \(\phi\) is uniformly distributed over \((0,T)\). Hence, \[f_{\phi}(\phi)=\frac{1}{T}, \qquad 0<\phi<T\]If \(t_i\) and \(t_j\) lie on the same pulse, then Case (i): \[KT+\phi<t_i\] \[(K+1)T+\phi>t_j\]Therefore, \[\phi<t_i-KT\]and \[\phi>t_j-(K+1)T\]Hence, \[E[p(t_i-nT-\phi)\,p(t_j-nT-\phi)] = \int_{t_j-(K+1)T}^{\,t_i-KT} \left(\frac{1}{T}\right)d\phi\] \[= 1-\frac{t_j-t_i}{T}\]Similarly for Case(ii), [figure unavailable] \[E[p(t_i-nT-\phi)\,p(t_j-nT-\phi)] = 1-\frac{t_i-t_j}{T}\]Let, \[\tau=t_j-t_i\]Then, \[R_{yy}(t_i,t_j)=R_{yy}(\tau)\] \[= E[y(t)y(t+\tau)]\]Using (2), \[R_{yy}(\tau) = E[X_i^2] \left( 1-\frac{|\tau|}{T} \right), \qquad |\tau|\le T\] \[= 1\left( 1-\frac{|\tau|}{T} \right)\]Now, \[\tau=\frac{3T}{4}\]Therefore, \[R_{yy}\left(\frac{3T}{4}\right) = 1\left( 1-\frac{3T/4}{T} \right)\] \[= 1\left(1-\frac34\right)\] \[= 0.25\] \[\boxed{ R_{yy}\left(\frac{3T}{4}\right)=0.25 }\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: The input \(X\) to the Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) shown in the figure is `\(1\)' with probability \(0.8\). The cross-over probability is \(\dfrac{1}{7}\). If the received bit \(Y=0\), the conditional probability that `\(1\)' was transmitted is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: Theory: Since the received symbol is known, the probability that a particular symbol was transmitted is obtained using Bayes' theorem. Given, \[P(X=1)=0.8,\] \[P(X=0)=0.2,\]and the crossover probability of the BSC is \[p=\frac{1}{7}.\]Hence, \[P(Y=0|X=1)=\frac{1}{7},\] \[P(Y=0|X=0)=\frac{6}{7}.\] [figure unavailable] Using Bayes' theorem, \[P(X=1|Y=0) = \frac{P(Y=0|X=1)\,P(X=1)} {P(Y=0)}.\]Now, \[P(Y=0) = P(Y=0|X=1)P(X=1) + P(Y=0|X=0)P(X=0).\]Substituting the values, \[P(X=1|Y=0) = \frac{\left(\frac{1}{7}\right)(0.8)} {\left(\frac{1}{7}\right)(0.8)+\left(\frac{6}{7}\right)(0.2)}.\] \[= \frac{0.8} {0.8+1.2}.\] \[= \frac{0.8}{2}.\]Therefore, \[\boxed{P(X=1|Y=0)=0.4}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question:
A source emits bit \(0\) with probability \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and bit \(1\) with probability \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). The emitted bits are communicated to the receiver. The receiver decides for either \(0\) or \(1\) based on the received value \(R\). It is given that the conditional density functions of \(R\) are as \[f_{R|0}(r)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{4}, & -3 \leq x \leq 1, \\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\] \[f_{R|1}(r)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{6}, & -1 \leq x \leq 5, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\]The minimum decision error probability is.
questions.explanation: Theory: For minimum probability of error, the MAP detector chooses the symbol having the larger weighted likelihood, i.e., likelihood multiplied by its prior probability. Given, \[P(s_0)=\frac{1}{3}, \qquad P(s_1)=\frac{2}{3}.\]The conditional PDFs are [figure unavailable] \[f_R(r|s_0)=\frac{1}{4}, \qquad -3 \le r \le 1,\] \[f_R(r|s_1)=\frac{1}{6}, \qquad -1 \le r \le 5.\]Including the prior probabilities, \[f_R(r|s_0)P(s_0) = \frac{1}{4}\times\frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{12},\] \[f_R(r|s_1)P(s_1) = \frac{1}{6}\times\frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{9}.\]Since \[\frac{1}{9}>\frac{1}{12},\]the detector should decide in favor of \(s_1\) throughout the overlap region \(-1 \le r \le 1\). Hence the optimum threshold is \[r_{\text{th}}=-1.\] [figure unavailable] For \(r_{\text{th}}=-1\), \[P(r_0|s_1)P(s_1)=0,\]because the entire support of \(f_R(r|s_1)\) lies to the right of \(-1\). The only contribution to error comes from deciding \(s_1\) when \(s_0\) was transmitted: \[P(r_1|s_0)P(s_0) = \frac{1}{12} \left[\,1-(-1)\,\right].\] \[= \frac{1}{12}(2) = \frac{1}{6}.\]Therefore, \[P_{e(\min)} = P(r_0|s_1)P(s_1) + P(r_1|s_0)P(s_0)\] \[= 0+\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{6}.\] \[\boxed{(D) P_{e(\min)}=\frac{1}{6}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: The transmitted signal in a GSM system is of \(200\ \text{kHz}\) bandwidth and \(8\) users share a common bandwidth using TDMA. If at a given time \(12\) users are talking in a cell, the total bandwidth of the signal received by the base station of the cell will be at least (in kHz) .
questions.explanation: Theory: In TDMA, multiple users share the same carrier bandwidth by transmitting in different time slots. Hence one GSM carrier of \(200\,\text{kHz}\) can support \(8\) users. Given, \[\text{Bandwidth per GSM carrier} = 200~\text{kHz}\] \[\text{Number of users supported per carrier} = 8\] \[\text{Number of active users} = 12\]Since one carrier can accommodate only \(8\) users, \(12\) users require \[\left\lceil \frac{12}{8} \right\rceil = 2\]GSM carriers. Therefore, the total bandwidth required is \[B_{\text{total}} = 2 \times 200 = 400~\text{kHz}\]Hence, \[\boxed{B_{\text{total}} = 400~\text{kHz}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: Consider a binary digital communication system which uses pulses \(g(t)\) and \(-g(t)\) for transmitting bits over an AWGN channel. If the receiver uses a matched filter, which one of the following pulses will give the minimum probability of bit error?
questions.explanation: Theory: For antipodal signaling \(\{g(t),-g(t)\}\) over an AWGN channel with a matched filter receiver, the probability of error decreases as the signal energy increases. Hence, we choose the pulse with the maximum energy. For a signal \(g(t)\), \[E=\int_{0}^{1} g^2(t)\,dt\] Option (A): Rectangular pulse \[g(t)=1,\qquad 0\le t\le 1\] \[E_A=\int_0^1 1^2\,dt =1\] Option (B): Triangular pulse \[g(t)= \begin{cases} 2t, & 0\le t\le \tfrac12\\ 2(1-t), & \tfrac12\le t\le 1 \end{cases}\] \[E_B = 2\int_0^{1/2}(2t)^2dt = 8\int_0^{1/2}t^2dt\] \[= 8\left[\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/2} = \frac{1}{3}\] Option (C): Decreasing ramp \[g(t)=1-t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1\] \[E_C = \int_0^1(1-t)^2dt = \frac{1}{3}\] Option (D): Increasing ramp \[g(t)=t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1\] \[E_D = \int_0^1 t^2dt = \frac{1}{3}\]Thus, \[E_A=1, \qquad E_B=E_C=E_D=\frac13\]Since \[E_A>E_B,E_C,E_D,\]the rectangular pulse provides the maximum SNR and hence the minimum probability of error. \[\boxed{\text{(A)}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A sinusoidal signal of amplitude \(A\) is quantized by a uniform quantizer. Assume that the signal utilizes all the representation levels of the quantizer. If the signal to quantization noise ratio is \(31.8\ \text{dB}\), the number of levels in the quantizer is .
questions.explanation: Theory: For a full-scale sinusoidal input applied to a uniform quantizer, the signal-to-quantization noise ratio (SQNR) is approximately \[\text{SQNR}_{\text{dB}} = 1.8 + 6n\]where \(n\) is the number of bits per sample. Given, \[\text{SQNR} = 31.8~\text{dB}\]Substituting into the SQNR formula, \[31.8 = 1.8 + 6n\] \[6n = 30\] \[n = 5\]The number of quantization levels is \[L = 2^n\] \[L = 2^5\] \[\boxed{L = 32}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A sinusoidal signal of \(2\ \text{kHz}\) frequency is applied to a delta modulator. The sampling rate and step-size \(\Delta\) of the delta modulator are \(20,000\) samples per second and \(0.1\ \text{V}\), respectively. To prevent slope overload, the maximum amplitude of the sinusoidal signal (in Volts) is
questions.explanation: Theory: To avoid slope overload distortion in a delta modulator, the maximum slope of the input signal must not exceed the maximum tracking slope of the modulator. For a sinusoidal signal, \[m(t)=A_m\sin(2\pi f_m t)\]the maximum slope is \[\left|\frac{dm(t)}{dt}\right|_{\max} = 2\pi f_m A_m.\]The maximum tracking slope of the delta modulator is \[\Delta f_s.\]Hence, for slope-overload-free operation, \[2\pi f_m A_m \le \Delta f_s.\]At the limiting condition, \[2\pi f_m A_m = \Delta f_s.\]Substituting the given values, \[2\pi (2000)\,A_m = (0.1)(20000).\] \[4000\pi\,A_m = 2000.\] \[A_m = \frac{2000}{4000\pi}.\] \[A_m = \frac{1}{2\pi}\ \text{V}.\]Hence, the maximum permissible amplitude is \[\boxed{A_m=\frac{1}{2\pi}\ \text{V}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: In the system shown in Figure (a), \(m(t)\) is a low-pass signal with bandwidth \(W\) Hz. The frequency response of the band-pass filter \(H(f)\) is shown in Figure (b). If it is desired that the output signal \(z(t)=10x(t)\), the maximum value of \(W\) (in Hz) should be strictly less than [figure unavailable] [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Theory: To recover only \(10x(t)\) at the output, the spectrum generated by the nonlinear term \(x^2(t)\) must lie completely outside the passband of the filter. Given, \[x(t)=m(t)\cos(2400\pi t).\]Since \[2400\pi = 2\pi f_c,\]we obtain \[f_c=1200~\text{Hz}.\] [figure unavailable] The amplifier output is \[y(t)=10x(t)+x^2(t).\]Substituting \(x(t)\),\[y(t) = 10m(t)\cos(2400\pi t) + m^2(t)\cos^2(2400\pi t).\]Using\[\cos^2\theta = \frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2},\]\[y(t) = 10m(t)\cos(2400\pi t) + \frac{m^2(t)}{2} + \frac{m^2(t)}{2}\cos(4800\pi t).\]Thus \(y(t)\) contains three spectral components:
  1. Baseband term \[\frac{m^2(t)}{2}\] with bandwidth \(2W\).
  2. Desired bandpass term \[10m(t)\cos(2400\pi t)\] centered at \(1200\) Hz with bandwidth \(W\).
  3. Undesired term \[\frac{m^2(t)}{2}\cos(4800\pi t)\]centered at \(2400\) Hz with bandwidth \(2W\).
[figure unavailable] The desired spectrum occupies \[1200-W \le f \le 1200+W.\]Since the filter passband is \[700 \le |f| \le 1700,\]the entire desired spectrum must remain inside the passband. Hence, \[1200-W > 700\] \[W<500.\]Also, \[1200+W <1700\] \[W<500.\] Now consider the baseband component arising from \[\frac{m^2(t)}{2}.\]Its bandwidth is \[2W.\]To prevent it from entering the filter passband, \[2W<700.\]Therefore, \[W<350.\] Next consider the high-frequency component \[\frac{m^2(t)}{2}\cos(4800\pi t).\]Its spectrum extends from \[2400-2W\]to \[2400+2W.\]To keep it completely outside the passband, \[2400-2W>1700.\]Thus, \[700>2W\] \[W<350.\] Combining all constraints, \[W<500, \qquad W<350, \qquad W<350.\]Hence, \[\boxed{W<350~\text{Hz}}.\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget that squaring a signal doubles its bandwidth. If \(m(t)\) has bandwidth \(W\), \[m^2(t)\] has bandwidth \[2W.\]
  • Always use \[\cos^2\theta = \frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}\] before drawing the spectrum.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.ref: Coordinate Geometry & Maxwell's Equation - Basics Q1
questions.question: A vector field \(\vec{D} = 2\rho^2 \hat{a}_\rho + z \hat{a}_z\) exists inside a cylindrical region enclosed by the surfaces \(\rho = 1\), \(z = 0\) and \(z = 5\). Let \(S\) be the surface bounding this cylindrical region. The surface integral of this field on \(S \oiint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s}\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given vector field: \[\vec{D} = 2\rho^2\hat{a}_{\rho} + z\hat{a}_{z}\] Surface bounds: \(\rho = 1\), \(z = 0\), and \(z = 5\).
Method 1
By evaluating the surface integral directly over the closed cylindrical surface: \[\oiint_{S} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int_{\text{Top surface}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} + \int_{\text{Bottom surface}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} + \int_{\text{Curved surface}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s}\] For the top surface (\(z = 5, \, \hat{a}_{n} = \hat{a}_{z}, \, d\vec{s} = \rho \, d\rho \, d\phi \, \hat{a}_{z}\)): \[\int_{\text{Top}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} (5) \rho \, d\rho \, d\phi = 5 (2\pi) \left[ \frac{\rho^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{1} = 5\pi\] For the bottom surface (\(z = 0, \, \hat{a}_{n} = -\hat{a}_{z}, \, d\vec{s} = -\rho \, d\rho \, d\phi \, \hat{a}_{z}\)): \[\int_{\text{Bottom}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} (-0) \rho \, d\rho \, d\phi = 0\] For the curved surface (\(\rho = 1, \, \hat{a}_{n} = \hat{a}_{\rho}, \, d\vec{s} = \rho \, d\phi \, dz \, \hat{a}_{\rho}\)): \[\int_{\text{Curved}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int_{0}^{5} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[2(1)^2\right] (1) \, d\phi \, dz = 2 (2\pi) (5) = 20\pi\] Summing the contributions: \[\oiint_{S} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = 5\pi + 0 + 20\pi = 25\pi \approx \boxed{78.54}\]
Method 2
Using Divergence Theorem: \[\oiint_{S} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \iiint_{V} (\nabla \cdot \vec{D}) \, dV\] In cylindrical coordinates: \[\nabla \cdot \vec{D} = \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} (\rho D_{\rho}) + \frac{\partial D_{z}}{\partial z}\] \[= \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} (2\rho^3) + \frac{\partial z}{\partial z}\] \[= 6\rho + 1\] Volume element: \[dV = \rho \, d\rho \, d\phi \, dz\] Limits of integration: \[0 \le \rho \le 1, \quad 0 \le \phi \le 2\pi, \quad 0 \le z \le 5\] Therefore: \[\oiint_{S} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \int_{0}^{5} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} (6\rho + 1) \rho \, d\rho \, d\phi \, dz\] \[= \int_{0}^{5} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} (6\rho^2 + \rho) \, d\rho \, d\phi \, dz\] \[= \left( 2 + \frac{1}{2} \right) (2\pi)(5)\] \[= \frac{5}{2} \times 10\pi = 25\pi \approx \boxed{78.54}\]
Key points
  • Gauss's Divergence Theorem states that the outward flux of a vector field through a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence of the field.
  • The total closed surface of a cylinder consists of three distinct parts: top disk, bottom disk, and the outer curved wall.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.ref: Coordinate Geometry & Maxwell's Equation - Basics Q2
questions.question: In a source free region in vacuum, if the electrostatic potential \(\phi = 2x^2 + y^2 + cz^2\), the value of constant \(c\) must be .
questions.explanation:
Given the electrostatic potential: \[\phi = 2x^2 + y^2 + cz^2\]
Method 1
By directly applying Laplace's equation in a source-free region: \[ abla^2\phi = 0\] In Cartesian coordinates, the Laplacian is given by: \[ rac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2} + rac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2} + rac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z^2} = 0\] Computing the second partial derivatives: \[ rac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}(2x^2 + y^2 + cz^2) = 4\] \[ rac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2}(2x^2 + y^2 + cz^2) = 2\] \[ rac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(2x^2 + y^2 + cz^2) = 2c\] Substituting these values back into Laplace's equation: \[4 + 2 + 2c = 0\] \[6 + 2c = 0\] \[c = -3\]
Method 2
Using Maxwell's first equation and the relationship between electric field and potential: In a source-free region, Gauss's Law states: \[ abla \cdot \vec{D} = 0 \implies \epsilon( abla \cdot \vec{E}) = 0 \implies abla \cdot \vec{E} = 0\] The electric field intensity \(\vec{E}\) is related to the potential by: \[\vec{E} = - abla V = - abla\phi\] Finding the gradient of the potential (\( abla\phi\)): \[ abla\phi = rac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}\hat{a}_{x} + rac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}\hat{a}_{y} + rac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\hat{a}_{z}\] \[-\vec{E} = 4x\hat{a}_{x} + 2y\hat{a}_{y} + 2cz\hat{a}_{z}\] \[\vec{E} = -4x\hat{a}_{x} - 2y\hat{a}_{y} - 2cz\hat{a}_{z}\] Applying the divergence condition \( abla \cdot \vec{E} = 0\): \[ rac{\partial E_{x}}{\partial x} + rac{\partial E_{y}}{\partial y} + rac{\partial E_{z}}{\partial z} = 0\] \[-4 - 2 - 2c = 0\] \[4 + 2 + 2c = 0\] \[c = -3\]
\[ oxed{-3}\]
Key points
  • Laplace's equation (\( abla^2\phi = 0\)) is used to find the potential distribution in static configurations inside charge-free domains.
  • The electric field is always conservative under static conditions, meaning it can be represented as the negative gradient of a scalar potential field (\(\vec{E} = - abla\phi\)).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The electric field of a plane wave propagating in a lossless non-magnetic medium is given by the following expression:\[\vec{E}(z,t) = \hat{a}_x 5 \cos(2\pi \times 10^9 t + \beta z)\]\[+\hat{a}_y 3 \cos\left(2\pi \times 10^9 t + \beta z - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\]The polarization of the wave is
questions.explanation:
The given electric field expression is: \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \hat{a}_{x} 5 \cos(2\pi \times 10^{9} t + \beta z) + \hat{a}_{y} 3 \cos\left(2\pi \times 10^{9} t + \beta z - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\] To determine the polarization state, we analyze the following characteristics:
  • Direction of Propagation: The argument of the cosine function is \((\omega t + \beta z)\). Since the signs of the \(t\) and \(z\) terms are the same, the wave is travelling in the \(-\hat{a}_{z}\) direction.
  • Amplitudes: The magnitudes of the orthogonal components are \(E_{x0} = 5\) and \(E_{y0} = 3\). Since \(E_{x0} \neq E_{y0}\), the polarization cannot be circular.
  • Phase Difference: The \(y\)-component lags the \(x\)-component by \(\phi = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
  • Handedness: At \(z = 0\), as time \(t\) increases from \(0\):
    • At \(t = 0\): \(\vec{E} = 5\hat{a}_{x} + 0\hat{a}_{y}\)
    • At \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\vec{E} = 0\hat{a}_{x} + 3\hat{a}_{y}\)
    The tip of the electric field vector moves from the positive \(x\)-axis toward the positive \(y\)-axis (counter-clockwise when looking in the \(+\hat{a}_{z}\) direction). Since the wave is propagating in the \(-\hat{a}_{z}\) direction, we point our thumb in the \(-\hat{a}_{z}\) direction. The fingers of the left hand curl in the direction of the field rotation.
Therefore, the wave is Left Hand Elliptically Polarized (LHEP). \[\boxed{\text{(B) Left hand elliptically polarized}}\]
Key points
  • For a wave propagating in the \(-z\) direction, if the field rotates from \(x\) to \(y\) (CCW), it is left-handed.
  • Elliptical polarization occurs when orthogonal components have unequal amplitudes and a phase difference of \(\pm 90^{\circ}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The electric field of a uniform plane electromagnetic wave is \[\vec{E} = (\hat{a}_x + j2\hat{a}_y) \exp[j(2\pi \times 10^7 t - 0.2z)]\]The polarization of the wave is
questions.explanation: The given electric field in phasor form is: \[\vec{E} = (\hat{a}_{x} + j2\hat{a}_{y}) \exp[j(\omega t - \beta z)]\] where \(\omega = 2\pi \times 10^{7}\,\text{rad/s}\) and \(\beta = 0.2\,\text{rad/m}\). The negative sign in the \((\omega t - \beta z)\) term indicates propagation in the \(+z\) direction. To find the instantaneous physical electric field, we convert it to the time-domain: \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \text{Re}\left\{ (\hat{a}_{x} + j2\hat{a}_{y}) e^{j(\omega t - \beta z)} \right\}\] Substituting \(j = e^{j\pi/2}\) into the \(y\)-component: \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \cos(\omega t - \beta z)\hat{a}_{x} + 2\cos\left(\omega t - \beta z + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\hat{a}_{y}\] \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \cos(\omega t - \beta z)\hat{a}_{x} - 2\sin(\omega t - \beta z)\hat{a}_{y}\] Analyzing the components \(E_{x}\) and \(E_{y}\): Because there is a \(90^{\circ}\) phase difference and the amplitudes are unequal (\(1 \neq 2\)), the tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse. To determine handedness, observe the vector rotation at a fixed plane (\(z = 0\)) as \(t\) increases: \[\vec{E}(0,t) = \cos(\omega t)\hat{a}_{x} - 2\sin(\omega t)\hat{a}_{y}\] At \(\omega t = 0\), \(\vec{E} = 1\hat{a}_{x}\). At \(\omega t = \pi/2\), \(\vec{E} = -2\hat{a}_{y}\). The vector rotates from the \(+x\)-axis to the \(-y\)-axis. Looking along the direction of wave propagation (\(+z\)-axis), this clockwise rotation corresponds to a left-handed polarization. \[\boxed{\text{(D) Left-handed elliptical}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The electric field intensity of a plane wave travelling in free space is given by the following expression: \[\vec{E}(x, t) = \hat{a}_y 24\pi \cos(\omega t - k_o x) \text{ V/m}\]In this field, consider a square area \(10 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}\) on a plane \(x + y = 1\). The total time averaged power (in \(mW\)) passing through the square area is ________.
questions.explanation:
We have an electric field given by: \[\mathbf{E}(x, t) = 24\pi \cos(\omega t - k_0 x)\mathbf{\hat{a}}_y\] Average Poynting vector: \[\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{E_o^2}{\eta_o} \mathbf{\hat{a}}_x\] \[\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{(24\pi)^2}{120\pi} \mathbf{\hat{a}}_x = 7.539 \mathbf{\hat{a}}_x\] We have unit normal to plane \(f = x + y - 1\) given by \[\mathbf{\hat{a}}_u = \frac{\nabla f}{|\nabla f|} = \frac{\mathbf{\hat{a}}_x + \mathbf{\hat{a}}_y}{\sqrt{2}}\] Now, the component of \(\mathbf{P} = 7.539 \mathbf{\hat{a}}_x\) along \(\mathbf{\hat{a}}_u\) is \[P_n = \mathbf{P} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{a}}_u = 7.539 \mathbf{\hat{a}}_x \cdot \left( \frac{\mathbf{\hat{a}}_x + \mathbf{\hat{a}}_y}{\sqrt{2}} \right)\] \[P_n = \frac{7.539}{\sqrt{2}} = 5.331\] Now, power passing through \(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\) area plate is \[W_E = 5.331 \times 100 \times 10^{-4}\] \[W_E = 53.31\text{ mW}\] \[\boxed{53.31}\]
Key points
  • The time-averaged power density for a plane wave is \(\vec{P}_{avg} = \frac{1}{2} \text{Re} \{ \vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*} \} = \frac{|E|^{2}}{2\eta} \hat{a}_{k}\).
  • Total power through a surface is the flux of the Poynting vector: \(P = \iint \vec{P} \cdot d\vec{s}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Consider a uniform plane wave with amplitude \((E_0)\) of \(10\text{ V/m}\) and \(1.1\text{ GHz}\) frequency travelling an air, and incident normally on a dielectric medium with complex relative permittivity \((\varepsilon_r)\) and permeability \((\mu_r)\) as shown in figure.[figure unavailable] The magnitude of the transmitted electric field component (in V/m) after it has travelled a distance of \(10\text{ cm}\) inside the dielectric region is ________.
questions.explanation:
The material is characterized by complex relative permeability \(\mu_{R}\) and complex relative permittivity \(\epsilon_{R}\). Since the material is a dielectric, the conductivity \(\sigma = 0\). The intrinsic impedance \(\eta\) of the material is given by: \[\eta = \sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma + j\omega\epsilon}} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{o}\mu_{R}}{\epsilon_{o}\epsilon_{R}}} = 120\pi\] Given that there are no reflections at the boundary, we calculate the propagation constant \(\gamma\): \[\gamma = \sqrt{j\omega\mu_{o}\mu_{R}(0 + j\omega\epsilon_{o}\epsilon_{R})}\] \[\gamma = j\omega\sqrt{\mu_{o}\epsilon_{o}\mu_{R}\epsilon_{R}}\] From the provided derivation, the propagation constant simplifies to include the attenuation constant \(\alpha\): \[\gamma = j\omega\sqrt{\mu_{o}\epsilon_{o}} + 2\omega\sqrt{\mu_{o}\epsilon_{o}}\] Thus, the attenuation constant is: \[\alpha = 2\omega\sqrt{\mu_{o}\epsilon_{o}} = 46.07\,\text{Np/m}\] The magnitude of the transmitted electric field component at a distance \(z = 0.1\,\text{m}\) is calculated as: \[|E| = E_{o} e^{-\alpha z}\] Substituting the values: \[|E| = E_{o} e^{-(46.07 \times 0.1)}\] Based on the image data, the resulting magnitude is: \[|E| = 0.1\,\text{V/m}\] \[\boxed{0.1}\]
Key points
  • The intrinsic impedance \(\eta\) for a lossless medium is \(120\pi \sqrt{\mu_{R}/\epsilon_{R}}\).
  • The propagation constant \(\gamma = \alpha + j\beta\) defines the attenuation (\(\alpha\)) and phase shift (\(\beta\)) of the wave.
  • The electric field magnitude decays exponentially in a lossy medium according to \(e^{-\alpha z}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The electric field component of a plane wave travelling in lossless dielectric medium is given by \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \hat{a}_y 2 \cos\left(10^8 t - \frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \text{ V/m}\]The wavelength (in m) for the wave is ________.
questions.explanation: The given electric field of the uniform plane wave is: \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \hat{a}_{y} 2 \cos\left( 10^{8} t - \frac{z}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \text{V/m}\] The general form of a plane wave propagating in the \(+z\) direction is: \[\vec{E}(z,t) = \hat{a}_{y} E_{o} \cos(\omega t - \beta z) \text{V/m}\] By comparing the given equation with the general form, we identify the phase constant \(\beta\): \[\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ rad/m}\] The relationship between the phase constant \(\beta\) and the wavelength \(\lambda\) is given by: \[\beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\] Rearranging to solve for the wavelength \(\lambda\): \[\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{\beta} = \frac{2\pi}{1/\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\pi \text{ m}\] Calculating the numerical value: \[\lambda \approx 8.88 \text{ m}\] \[\boxed{8.88}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A \(200 \text{ m}\) long transmission line having parameters shown in the figure is terminated into a load \(R_L\). The line is connected to a \(400 \text{ V}\) source having source \(R_s\) through a switch which is closed at \(t = 0\). The transient response of the circuit at the input of the line (\(z = 0\)) is also drawn in the figure. [figure unavailable] The value of \(R_L\) (in \(\Omega\)) is _____.
questions.explanation:
To find the load resistance \(R_{L}\) of the transmission line, we analyze the voltage behavior at the input over time. Given the source voltage \(V_s = 400\,\text{V}\), source resistance \(R_s = 150\,\Omega\), and characteristic impedance \(R_0 = 50\,\Omega\). At \(t=0\), the initial input voltage \(V_{in}(0)\) is determined by the voltage divider between \(R_0\) and \(R_s\): \[V_{in} = V_s \times \frac{R_0}{R_0 + R_s} = 400 \times \frac{50}{50 + 150} = 400 \times \frac{50}{200} = 100\,\text{V}\] At \(t = 2T_0\) (where \(T_0\) is the one-way travel time), the input voltage is affected by reflections at both the load (\(\Gamma_L\)) and the source (\(\Gamma_{in}\)): \[V_{in}(2T_0) = V_{in}(0) + V_{in}(0) \cdot \Gamma_L \cdot (1 + \Gamma_{in}) = 62.5\,\text{V}\] \[100 + 100 \cdot \Gamma_L \cdot (1 + \Gamma_{in}) = 62.5\] \[100 \cdot \Gamma_L \cdot (1 + \Gamma_{in}) = -37.5\] Assuming \(\Gamma_{in} = \frac{R_s - R_0}{R_s + R_0} = \frac{150 - 50}{150 + 50} = \frac{100}{200} = 0.5\): \[100 \cdot \Gamma_L \cdot (1 + 0.5) = -37.5\] \[150 \cdot \Gamma_L = -37.5 \implies \Gamma_L = -\frac{37.5}{150} = -0.25 = -\frac{1}{4}\] Using the definition of the load reflection coefficient: \[\Gamma_L = \frac{R_L - R_0}{R_L + R_0}\] \[-\frac{1}{4} = \frac{R_L - 50}{R_L + 50}\] \[-(R_L + 50) = 4(R_L - 50)\] \[-R_L - 50 = 4R_L - 200\] \[5R_L = 150 \implies R_L = 30\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{30}\]
Key points
  • Reflection Coefficient (\(\Gamma\)): Quantifies the impedance mismatch at junctions; \(\Gamma = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)\).
  • Bouncing Diagram Method: Useful for tracking multiple reflections on a transmission line over discrete time intervals (\(2T_0, 4T_0, \dots\)).
  • Input Impedance: The observed voltage changes at the input are a function of the wave traveling back and forth along the line.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the source reflection coefficient (\(\Gamma_{in}\)) is calculated using the source resistance, not the load resistance.
  • Pay close attention to the time delay; the reflection returns to the input only after a round trip (\(2T_0\)).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A coaxial capacitor of inner radius \(1 \text{ mm}\) and outer radius \(5 \text{ mm}\) has a capacitance a per unit length of \(172 \text{ pF/m}\). If the ratio of outer radius to inner is doubled, the capacitance per unit length (in \(\text{pF/m}\)) is _____.
questions.explanation: \[C = \frac{Q}{V}, \text{ where } C \text{ is the capacitance}\] \[Q \text{ is the Charge} = \oint E \cdot ds\] \[V \text{ is the Potential Difference} = -\int E \cdot dl\] \[Q = \epsilon \oint E \cdot ds = \epsilon E \cdot 2\pi\rho L \quad (a < \rho < b) \quad \dots 1)\] \[V = -\int E \cdot dl\] From 1): \[V = -\int_{b}^{a} \frac{Q}{2\pi\epsilon L\rho} \cdot d\rho = -\frac{Q}{2\pi\epsilon L} [\ln \rho]_{b}^{a} = \frac{Q}{2\pi\epsilon L} \ln \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\] \[\Rightarrow V = \frac{Q}{2\pi\epsilon L} \ln \left(\frac{b}{a}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{2\pi\epsilon L}{\ln \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)} \quad \dots 2)\] \[C_1 = 172 = \frac{2\pi\epsilon L}{\ln\left(\frac{5}{1}\right)} \quad (\text{Given})\] When the inner radius is doubled, \[C_2 = \frac{2\pi\epsilon L}{\ln(10)}\] Divide both these equations: \[\frac{C_1}{C_2} = \frac{172}{C_2} = \frac{\ln 10}{\ln 5} \Rightarrow C_2 = \frac{\ln 5}{\ln 10} \times 172 \, \text{pF/m}\] \[\Rightarrow C_2 = 120.22 \, \text{pF/m}\] Hence the required capacitance \(= 120.22 \, \text{pF/m}\) \[\boxed{120.22}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Consider the \(3 \text{ m}\) long lossless air-filled transmission line shown in the figure. It has a characteristic impedance of \(120 \pi \, \Omega\), is terminated by a short-circuit, and is excited with a frequency of \(37.5 \text{ MHz}\). What is the nature of the input impedance (\(Z_{\text{in}}\))? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
To find the input impedance of a short-circuited lossy transmission line, we use the formula for the input impedance of a lossless line as a base, adjusted for the given parameters. The input impedance \(Z_{in}\) for a transmission line of length \(l\) terminated in a short circuit is: \[Z_{in} = j Z_0 \tan(\beta l)\] where \(Z_0\) is the characteristic impedance and \(\beta\) is the phase constant. Given: \[l = 3\,\text{m}\] \[f = 37.5\,\text{MHz} = 37.5 \times 10^6\,\text{Hz}\] The wavelength \(\lambda\) is calculated as: \[\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{37.5 \times 10^6\,\text{Hz}} = 8\,\text{m}\] The phase constant \(\beta\) is: \[\beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\,\text{rad/m}\] The argument for the tangent function is: \[\beta l = \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \times 3 = \frac{3\pi}{4}\,\text{rad}\] The characteristic impedance \(Z_0\) is typically \(120\pi\,\Omega\) for free space. \[Z_{in} = j (120\pi) \tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\] Since \(\tan(3\pi/4) = -1\): \[Z_{in} = j (120\pi) (-1) = -j 120\pi\,\Omega\] \[Z_{in} \approx -j 376.99\,\Omega \approx -j 377\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{(D):Capacitive}\]
Key points
  • Input Impedance of SC Line: A short-circuited transmission line section acts as an inductor or capacitor depending on its electrical length (\(l < \lambda/4 \implies\) inductive; \(\lambda/4 < l < \lambda/2 \implies\) capacitive).
  • Electrical Length: Calculated as \(\beta l = \frac{2\pi l}{\lambda}\), which determines the reactive nature of the line termination.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A co-axial cable is made of two brass conductors. The spacing between the conductors is filled with Teflon (\(\epsilon_r = 2.1, \tan\delta = 0\)). Which of the following circuits can represent the lumped element model of a small piece of this cable having length \(\Delta z\)?
questions.explanation:
The dielectric medium between the transmission lines is specified as Teflon. The loss tangent (\(\tan\delta\)) of a dielectric is defined as the ratio of the imaginary part of the permittivity to its real part, or alternatively, the ratio of conduction current to displacement current. Given: \[\tan\delta = 0\] For a dielectric medium, the conductance per unit length (\(G\)) is related to the loss tangent and the capacitance per unit length (\(C\)) by the expression: \[G = \omega C \tan\delta\] where \(\omega\) is the angular frequency. Since \(\tan\delta = 0\), it follows that: \[G = \omega C \cdot 0 = 0\] This indicates that the medium between the lines is lossless, meaning there is no shunt conductance causing energy dissipation within the dielectric. \[\boxed{(B)}\]
Key points
  • Loss Tangent (\(\tan\delta\)): Quantifies the energy dissipation in a dielectric material under an alternating electric field.
  • Lossless Dielectric: When \(\tan\delta = 0\), the medium is considered perfectly dielectric with zero conductivity (\(\sigma = 0\)), resulting in zero shunt conductance (\(G = 0\)).
  • Transmission Line Parameters: The primary line parameters (\(R, L, G, C\)) completely characterize a transmission line, where \(G\) represents dielectric losses.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: An air filled rectangular waveguide of interval dimensions \(a \text{ cm} \times b \text{ cm}\) (\(a > b\)) has a cut-off frequency of \(6 \text{ GHz}\) for the dominant \(\text{TE}_{10}\) mode. For the same waveguide, if the cut-off frequency of the \(\text{TM}_{11}\) mode is \(15 \text{ GHz}\), the cut-off frequency of the \(\text{TE}_{01}\) mode (in GHz) is ____.
questions.explanation: Given the cut-off frequency of the dominant \(TE_{10}\) mode is \(f_{c,TE_{10}} = 6\,\text{GHz}\), we determine the waveguide width \(a\): \[f_{c,TE_{10}} = \frac{c}{2a} = 6 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}\] \[a = \frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{2 \times 6 \times 10^{9}} = 2.5\,\text{cm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\] The cut-off frequency for the \(TM_{11}\) mode is given by: \[f_{c,TM_{11}} = \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} = 15\,\text{GHz} = 15 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}\] Substituting \(a = 2.5\,\text{cm}\): \[\frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{(2.5)^2} + \frac{1}{b^2}} = 15 \times 10^{9}\] \[\sqrt{\frac{1}{6.25} + \frac{1}{b^2}} = \frac{15 \times 10^9 \times 2}{3 \times 10^{10}} = 1\] \[\frac{1}{6.25} + \frac{1}{b^2} = 1 \implies \frac{1}{b^2} = 1 - \frac{1}{6.25} = \frac{5.25}{6.25}\] \[b = 2.5 / \sqrt{5.25}\] The cut-off frequency for the \(TE_{01}\) mode is: \[f_{c,TE_{01}} = \frac{c}{2b} = \frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{2 \times (2.5 / \sqrt{5.25})}\] \[f_{c,TE_{01}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{10} \times \sqrt{5.25}}{5} = 6 \times 10^{9} \times \sqrt{5.25} \approx 13.75\,\text{GHz}\] \[\boxed{13.75}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The longitudinal component of the magnetic field inside an air filled rectangular waveguide made of a perfect electric conductor is given by the following expression: \(H_z(x, y, z, t) = 0.1 \cos(25\pi x) \cos(30.3\pi y) \cos(12\pi \times 10^9 t - \beta z) \text{ A/m}\) The cross-sectional dimensions of the waveguide are given as \(a = 0.08 \text{ m}\) and \(b = 0.033 \text{ m}\). The mode of propagation inside the waveguide is
questions.explanation: The given axial magnetic field component is: \[H_{z}(x, y, z, t) = 0.1 \cos\left(25\pi x\right) \cos\left(30.3\pi y\right) \cos\left(12\pi \times 10^{9}t - \beta z\right)\,\text{A/m}\] For a rectangular waveguide of dimensions \(a = 0.08\,\text{m}\) and \(b = 0.033\,\text{m}\), the mode is identified as \(TE_{mn}\). The general form for the axial component of a \(TE_{mn}\) mode is proportional to \(\cos\left(\frac{m\pi x}{a}\right) \cos\left(\frac{n\pi y}{b}\right)\). Comparing the arguments of the cosine terms with the given equation: \[\frac{m\pi}{a} = 25\pi \implies \frac{m}{0.08} = 25 \implies m = 25 \times 0.08 = 2\] \[\frac{n\pi}{b} = 30.3\pi \implies \frac{n}{0.033} = 30.3 \implies n = 30.3 \times 0.033 \approx 1\] Thus, the propagating mode is \(TE_{21}\). \[\boxed{(C):TE_{21}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The directivity of an antenna array can be increased by adding more antenna elements, as a larger number of elements
options: increases the effective area of the antenna
results in a better impedance matching
allows more power to be transmitted by the antenna
questions.explanation: The relationship between effective aperture area (\(A_{e}\)) and directivity (\(D\)) for an antenna is given by: \[A_{e} = \frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi} D\] From this fundamental relationship, it is evident that for a fixed operating wavelength (\(\lambda\)): \[A_{e} \propto D\] This means that an increase in directivity (\(D \uparrow\)) directly corresponds to an increase in the effective area (\(A_{e} \uparrow\)) of the antenna system. In practical antenna arrays, this is achieved by increasing the number of radiating elements, which narrows the beamwidth and consequently enhances both directivity and effective aperture. \[\boxed{\text{Increases the effective area of the antenna}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Two half-wave dipole antennas placed as shown in the figure are excited with sinusoidally varying currents of frequency \(3 \text{ MHz}\) and phase shift of \(\pi/2\) between them (the element at the origin leads in phase). If the maximum radiated \(E\) field at the point \(P\) in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane occurs at an azimuthal angle of \(60^\circ\), the distance \(d\) (in meters) between the antenna is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The total electric field is given by: [figure unavailable] \[\vec{E}_{s} = \frac{I_{0} \, dl \sin \theta \, e^{-j\beta r}}{4\pi r} (j\beta) \hat{a}_{r} \left[ e^{j0} e^{j\beta(0)} + e^{-j\pi/2} e^{j\beta(d \hat{a}_{x} \cdot \hat{a}_{r})} \right]\] The array factor (A.F.) is: \[\text{A.F.} = \left[ 1 + e^{-j \pi/2} e^{j \beta d/2} \right]\] Given frequency \(f = 3\,\text{MHz}\), the wavelength \(\lambda\) is: \[\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{3 \times 10^{6}} = 100\,\text{m}\] [figure unavailable] The term \(\hat{a}_{x} \cdot \hat{a}_{r} = \sin \theta \cos \phi = \sin(\pi/2) \cos(60^{\circ}) = 1/2\). For maxima, the phase difference is: \[\psi = \beta d/2 - \pi/2 = 2n\pi\] \[d = \frac{(4n+1)\pi}{2\beta} = \frac{(4n+1)}{2} \lambda\] Evaluating for different values of \(n\): \[n=0 \implies d = \lambda/2 = 100/2 = 50\,\text{m}\] \[n=1 \implies d = 5\lambda/2\] \[n=-1 \implies d = -3\lambda/2 \text{ (Not possible)}\] Alternatively, if phase difference is \(\psi = \pi/2 - \beta d/2 = 2n\pi\): \[\beta d/2 = \pi/2 - 2n\pi = (1-4n) \frac{\pi}{2}\] \[d = (1-4n) \frac{\lambda}{2}\] Evaluating for this case: \[n=0 \implies d = \lambda/2 = 50\,\text{m}\] \[n=1 \implies d = -3\lambda/2 \text{ (Not possible)}\] \[n=-1 \implies d = 5\lambda/2\] \[\boxed{50}\]
Key points
  • The general phase expression \(\Psi = \beta(\vec{d} \cdot \hat{r}) + \alpha\) is robust regardless of the coordinate axis orientation.
  • For maximum radiation, the progressive phase shift \(\alpha\) must counteract the spatial phase lag induced by the geometry.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Failing to convert phase \(\alpha\) from degrees to radians when using \(\beta\) in rad/m.
  • Incorrectly identifying the angle \(\theta\) relative to the array axis.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence. The principal presented the chief guest with a , as token of appreciation.
questions.explanation:
The sentence describes presenting a token of appreciation — the blank requires a word meaning a keepsake or souvenir.

  • C. momentum — physics term for mass \(\times\) velocity; unrelated.
  • D. moment — a point in time; unrelated to tokens of appreciation.
\[\boxed{\text{B) memento}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the appropriate word/phrase, out of the four options given below, to complete the following sentence: Frogs .

The blank requires the sound that frogs make.
  • A. croak — the correct sound frogs make. \(\checkmark\) But check options.
  • B. roar — sound of lions.

  • D. patter — a light tapping sound; not associated with frogs.

Educe means to bring out or derive something from data/evidence — closest in meaning to Extract (to draw out or derive)
  • A. Exert — to apply effort; unrelated.
  • B. Educate — to teach

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The following question presents a sentence, part of which is underlined. Beneath the sentence you find four ways of phrasing the underlined part. Following the requirements of the standard written English, select the answer that produces the most effective sentence. Tuberculosis, together with its effects, <u>ranks one of the</u> <u>leading causes of death</u> in India.
options: ranks as one of the leading causes of death
rank as one of the leading causes of death
has the rank of one of the leading causes of death
are one of the leading causes of death
questions.explanation:
The subject ``Tuberculosis, together with its effects'' — the core subject is Tuberculosis (singular). ``Together with'' does not create a plural subject. The verb must be third-person singular.
  • A. ranks as one of the leading causes of death — singular verb; grammatically correct. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. rank as one of the leading causes of death — plural verb; incorrect.
  • C. ranked as one of the leading causes of death — past tense; incorrect for a general statement.
  • D. rank one of the leading causes of death — missing as; ungrammatical.
\[\boxed{\text{A) ranks as one of the leading causes of death}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Read the following paragraph and choose the correct statement. Climate change has reduced human security and threatened human well being. An ignored reality of human progress is that human security largely depends upon environmental security. But on the contrary, human progress seems contradictory to environmental security. To keep up both at the required level is a challenge to be addressed by one and all. One of the ways to curb the climate change may be suitable scientific innovations, while the other may be the Gandhian perspective on small scale progress with focus on sustainability.
options: Human progress and security are positively associated with environmental security.
Human progress is contradictory to environmental security.
Human security is contradictory to environmental security.
Human progress depends upon environmental security.
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided passage, let us analyze the relationships described:
  • The text mentions an ignored reality: "human security largely depends upon environmental security."
  • However, it immediately introduces a contrasting reality about progress: "But on the contrary, human progress seems contradictory to environmental security."
Let us evaluate the choices against these statements:
  • Option A: Incorrect. Human progress is explicitly stated to be contradictory, not positively associated.
  • Option B: Correct. This directly echoes the literal sentence from the passage: "human progress seems contradictory to environmental security."
  • Option C: Incorrect. The passage states human security depends upon environmental security, not that it is contradictory to it.
  • Option D: Incorrect. The passage states that human security (not human progress) depends upon environmental security.
\[\boxed{\text{B) Human progress is contradictory to environmental security.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Humpty Dumpty sits on a wall every day while having lunch. The wall sometimes breaks. A person sitting on the wall falls if the wall breaks. Which one of the statements below is logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentences?
options: Humpty Dumpty always falls while having lunch
Humpty Dumpty does not fall sometimes while having lunch
Humpty Dumpty never falls during dinner
When Humpty Dumpty does not sit on the wall, the wall does not break
questions.explanation:
Let us evaluate the statements step by step based on strict logical constraints provided in the premise:
  • Premise 1: Humpty Dumpty sits on a wall every day while having lunch.
  • Premise 2: The wall sometimes breaks.
  • Premise 3: A person sitting on the wall falls if the wall breaks (\(\text{Wall breaks} \rightarrow \text{Person falls}\)).
Let us analyze the logical validity of each choice:
  • Option A: Incorrect. Because the wall only breaks sometimes, Humpty Dumpty will only fall on the days when the wall breaks. He does not fall always.
  • Option B: Correct. Since the wall breaks only sometimes, it implies that on the remaining days, the wall does not break. If the wall does not break, Humpty Dumpty does not fall on those specific days. Thus, he does not fall sometimes while having lunch.
  • Option C: Incorrect. The passage provides zero information regarding what happens during dinner.
  • Option D: Incorrect. This assumes an inverse relationship (\(\neg \text{Condition} \rightarrow \neg \text{Consequence}\)). The premise states that if a person sits on it and it breaks, they fall, but it does not claim that a person sitting on it is the single cause behind the wall breaking.
\[\boxed{\text{B)Humpty Dumpty does not fall sometimes while having lunch}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the appropriate word/phrase, out of the four options given below, to complete the following sentence: Dhoni, as well as the other team members of Indian team, present on the occasion.
questions.explanation:
The subject is ``Dhoni, as well as the other team members of Indian team'' — the core subject is Dhoni (singular). ``As well as'' does not create a compound subject.
  • A. were — plural; incorrect.
  • B. was — singular past; correct. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. has — present perfect auxiliary; tense mismatch.
  • D. have — plural; incorrect.
\[\boxed{\text{B) was}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to the given word: Awkward
questions.explanation:
Awkward means clumsy, lacking grace or skill. The closest synonym:
  • A. Inept — lacking skill; very close in meaning. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. Graceful — antonym.
  • C. Suitable — unrelated.
  • D. Dreadful — means terrible; not synonymous with awkward.
\[\boxed{\text{A) Inept}}\]
Key points
  • Awkward \(\approx\) clumsy, inept, ungainly. Graceful is its antonym.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: What is the adverb for the given word below? Misogynous
questions.explanation:
The adverb form of Misogynous (adjective meaning hostile toward women):
  • A. Misogynousness — noun form.
  • B. Misogynity — not a standard word.
  • C. Misogynously — adverb form; adjective + -ly. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. Misogynous — original adjective; not the adverb.
\[\boxed{\text{C) Misogynously}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Assuming these statements to be true, decide which one logically follows. Statements:
  • I. All film stars are playback singers.
  • II. All film directors are film stars.
Conclusions:
  • I. All film directors are playback singers.
  • II. Some film stars are film directors.
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows.
Both conclusions I and II follow.
questions.explanation:
Statements:
  1. All film stars are playback singers.
  2. All film directors are film stars.
From I and II: All film directors are film stars (II), and all film stars are playback singers (I), so: \[\text{Film directors} \subset \text{Film stars} \subset \text{Playback singers}\] Conclusion I: All film directors are playback singers — TRUE (transitive). \(\checkmark\) Conclusion II: Some film stars are film directors — TRUE (since all film directors are film stars, film directors form a subset of film stars). \(\checkmark\) \[\boxed{\text{D) Both conclusions I and II follow}}\]
Key points
  • Transitivity: If \(A \subset B\) and \(B \subset C\), then \(A \subset C\).
  • If all A are B, then some B are A (conversion of universal affirmative).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Lamenting the gradual sidelining of the arts in school curricula, a group of prominent artists wrote to the Chief Minister last year, asking him to allocate more funds to support arts education in schools. However, no such increase has been announced in this year's Budget. The artists expressed their deep anguish at their request not being approved, but many of them remain optimistic about funding in the future. Which of the statement(s) below is/are logically valid and can be inferred from the above statements?
  1. The artists expected funding for the arts to increase this year.
  2. The Chief Minister was receptive to the idea of increasing funding for the arts.
  3. The Chief Minister is a prominent artist.
  4. Schools are giving less importance to arts education nowadays.
questions.explanation:
The passage describes artists writing to the Chief Minister requesting arts funding, being denied, yet remaining optimistic. Evaluate each statement:
  1. Artists expected funding to increase this year — they remain optimistic about future funding. \(\checkmark\)
  2. Chief Minister was receptive to increasing funding — not stated; no increase was announced.
  3. Chief Minister is a prominent artist — not stated.
  4. Schools are giving less importance to arts education — directly supported by ``the gradual sidelining of arts in school curricula''. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{B) (i) and (iv)}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence. If the athlete had wanted to come first in the race, he several hours every day.
questions.explanation:
The sentence describes a habitual past condition requiring practice — the athlete had wanted to come first, implying he should have practised (but didn't, or needed to have done so).
  • A. should practise — present; tense mismatch with had wanted.
  • B. should have practised — past modal perfect; correct for a missed obligation in the past. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. practised — simple past; grammatically incomplete without modal.
  • D. should be practising — present continuous; tense mismatch.
\[\boxed{\text{B) should have practised}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most suitable one word substitute for the following expression: Connotation of a road or way

Connotation of a road or way — a word meaning provision for a journey or travelling money/supplies:

  • B. Viaticum — provisions or money for a journey; directly related to a road/way. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. Clandestine — secret; unrelated.
  • D. Ravenous — extremely hungry; unrelated.
