questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the correct verb to fill in the blank below: Let us .
questions.explanation:
``Let us ____'' with the context of a group activity — the blank requires a verb meaning to take turns or act without bias.
  • A. introvert — become introverted; contextually wrong.
  • B. alternate — take turns; could fit depending on context. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. atheist — noun/adjective; wrong part of speech.
  • D. altruist — act selflessly for others; least appropriate for in context.
\[\boxed{\text{B) alternate}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Find the missing sequence in the letter series below: A, CD, GHI, ?, UVWXY
questions.explanation:
The given series follows two simultaneous patterns: the number of consecutive letters in each term increases by \(1\), and the number of skipped letters (gaps) between terms increases by \(1\). Step 1: Analyze Term Lengths
  • 1st Term: A \(\rightarrow\) \(1\) letter
  • 2nd Term: CD \(\rightarrow\) \(2\) letters
  • 3rd Term: GHI \(\rightarrow\) \(3\) letters
  • 4th Term: ? \(\rightarrow\) Should contain \(4\) letters
  • 5th Term: UVWXY \(\rightarrow\) \(5\) letters
Step 2: Analyze the Gaps Between Terms
Let us look at the missing letters between the consecutive blocks:
  • Between A and CD: B is skipped (\(1\) letter skipped)
  • Between CD and GHI: EF are skipped (\(2\) letters skipped)
  • Between GHI and ?: Following the pattern, \(3\) letters (JKL) must be skipped.
Step 3: Determine the Missing Term
Starting after the skipped letters JKL, the next \(4\) consecutive letters are: \[\text{\textbf{M, N, O, P}}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) MNOP}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Ram and Shyam shared a secret and promised to each other that it would remain between them. Ram expressed himself in one of the following ways as given in the choices below. Identify the correct way as per standard English.
options: It would remain between you and me.
It would remain between I and you.
It would remain between you and I.
questions.explanation:
Ram promises a secret ``would remain between you and me'' — uses objective case pronouns as objects of the preposition between.
  • A. It would remain between you and me
    — both pronouns in objective case; correct. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. between I and you — I is subjective; wrong after preposition.
  • C. between you and I — I after preposition is incorrect.
  • D. remain with me — changes meaning; excludes the other person.
\[\boxed{\text{A) It would remain between you and me}}\]
Key points
  • Prepositions take objective case: me, him, her, us, them — never I, he, she, we, they.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
In the following question, the first and the last sentence of the passage are in order and numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the passage is split into 4 parts and numbered as 2, 3, 4, and 5. These 4 parts are not arranged in proper order. Read the sentences and arrange them in a logical sequence to make a passage and choose the correct sequence from the given options.
  1. On Diwali, the family rises early in the morning.
  2. The whole family, including the young and the old enjoy doing this.
  3. Children let off fireworks later in the night with their friends.
  4. At sunset, the lamps are lit and the family performs various rituals.
  5. Father, mother, and children visit relatives and exchange gifts and sweets.
  6. Houses look so pretty with lighted lamps all around.
questions.explanation:
Sentence 1: On Diwali, the family rises early in the morning. Sentence 6: Houses look so pretty with lighted lamps all around. Logical sequence for a Diwali day narrative:
  1. Family rises early. (given)
  2. Father, mother, children visit relatives and exchange gifts. [5]
  3. At sunset, lamps are lit, family performs rituals. [2]
  4. Children let off fireworks later at night. [4]
  5. The whole family enjoys doing this. [3]
  6. Houses look pretty with lighted lamps. (given)
This gives the sequence: \(5, 2, 4, 3\). \[\boxed{\text{B) }5,\,2,\,4,\,3}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Ms.~X will be in Bagdogra from 01/05/2014 to 20/05/2014 and from 22/05/2014 to 31/05/2014. On the morning of 21/05/2014, she will reach Kochi via Mumbai. Which one of the statements below is logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentences?
options: Ms.~X will be in Kochi for one day, only in May.
Ms.~X will be in Kochi for only one day in May.
Ms.~X will be only in Kochi for one day in May.
Only Ms.~X will be in Kochi for one day in May.
questions.explanation:
Let us map out the timeline of Ms. X's schedule during the month of May 2014 step by step:
  • Bagdogra (First Stay): From 01/05/2014 to 20/05/2014 (Total 20 days).
  • Transit & Kochi Destination: On the morning of 21/05/2014, she travels and reaches Kochi via Mumbai. This fixes her presence in Kochi on 21/05/2014.
  • Bagdogra (Second Stay): From 22/05/2014 to 31/05/2014 (Total 10 days).
By analyzing this distribution, the entire month of May has 31 days. Out of these, 30 days are completely accounted for by her stays in Bagdogra (\(20 + 10 = 30\text{ days}\)). This leaves exactly one day remaining in the month: 21/05/2014. Therefore, she spends exactly one day in Kochi during the month of May. Let us evaluate the options to find the grammatically accurate statement that matching this deduction:
  • Option B: "Ms. X will be in Kochi for only one day in May." correctly and unambiguously states her duration of stay in Kochi for that month.
\[\boxed{\text {B) Ms. X will be in Kochi for only one day in May}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the appropriate word/phrase, out of the four options given below, to complete the following sentence: Apparent lifelessness dormant life.
questions.explanation:
``Apparent lifelessness ____ dormant life'' — the blank must connect lifelessness to dormant life with a verb meaning to contain or give way to.
  • A. harbours — to shelter or contain; fits perfectly (harbours dormant life). \(\checkmark\)
  • B. leads to — causes; possible but less precise.
  • C. supports — sustains; could fit.
  • D. affects — influences; changes meaning.
\[\boxed{\text{A) harbours}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct idiom/phrase. That boy from the town was a in the sleepy village.
questions.explanation:
The blank describes a person from a town who feels out of place in a sleepy village.
  • A. dog out of herd — not a standard idiom.
  • B. sheep from the heap— not a standard idiom.
  • C. fish out of water — someone in an unfamiliar or uncomfortable situation; correct. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. bird from the flock— not a standard idiom in this context.
\[\boxed{\text{C) fish out of water}}\]
Key points
  • Fish out of water = someone in an environment where they do not belong or feel uncomfortable.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the statement where underlined word is used correctly.
options: When the teacher eludes to different authors, he is being <u>elusive</u>.
When the thief keeps eluding the police, he is being <u>elusive</u>.
Matters that are difficult to understand, identify or remember are <u>allusive</u>.
Mirages can be <u>allusive</u>, but a better way to express them is illusory.
questions.explanation:
Distinguish elusive, eluding, and allusive:
  • elude/elusive = to escape or avoid.
  • allude/allusive = to make indirect reference to.
  • A. ``eludes to different authors'' — wrong; alludes to is correct (indirect reference).
  • B. ``eluding the police'' — correct; the thief avoids/escapes the police. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. ``are allusive'' — difficult things are not making allusions; should be elusive.
  • D. ``Mirages can be allusive'' — mirages are elusive (hard to grasp), not allusive (making references).
\[\boxed{\text{B) When the thief keeps eluding the police, he is being elusive}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Tanya is older than Eric. Cliff is older than Tanya. Eric is older than Cliff. If the first two statements are true, then the third statement is:
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Tanya is older than Eric.
  • Cliff is older than Tanya.
  • (Third statement to verify:) Eric is older than Cliff.
From statements 1 and 2: \[\text{Cliff} > \text{Tanya} > \text{Eric}\] The third statement says ``Eric is older than Cliff'' — this directly contradicts the chain above. \[\boxed{\text{B) False}}\]
Key points
  • Build the ordering chain from the first two statements, then test the third against it.
  • Cliff \(>\) Tanya \(>\) Eric contradicts Eric \(>\) Cliff directly.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Select the appropriate option in place of underlined part of the sentence. <u>Increased productivity necessary</u> reflects greater efforts made by the employees.
questions.explanation:
The sentence: ``Increased productivity necessary reflects greater efforts made by the employees.'' Necessary is misused as an adjective here — it should be necessarily (adverb) to modify the verb reflects:
  • A. Increase in productivity necessary — still uses adjective form.
  • B. Increase in productivity is necessary — changes meaning (makes a claim rather than an observation).
  • C. Increase in productivity necessarily — correct adverb modifying the verb. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. No improvement required — incorrect; error exists.
\[\boxed{\text{C) Increase in productivity necessarily reflects greater efforts made by the employees}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Assuming these statements to be true, decide which one logically follows. Statements:
  • I. No manager is a leader.
  • II. All leaders are executives.
Conclusions:
  • I. No manager is an executive.
  • II. No executive is a manager.
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows.
Both conclusions I and II follow.
questions.explanation:
Statements:
  1. No manager is a leader.
  2. All leaders are executives.
Conclusion I: No manager is an executive. From (i): managers \(\cap\) leaders \(= \emptyset\). From (ii): leaders \(\subset\) executives. But managers might still be executives through a path not involving leaders. Cannot conclude no manager is an executive. Does NOT follow. Conclusion II: No executive is a manager. Similar reasoning — no direct link established. Does NOT follow. \[\boxed{\text{C) Neither conclusion I nor II follows}}\]
Key points
  • ``No A is B'' and ``All B are C'' does not imply ``No A is C'' — A could be C via a different path.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Didn't you buy when you went shopping?
questions.explanation:
``Didn't you buy ____ when you went shopping?'' — a negative interrogative sentence typically expects any in standard English.
  • A. any paper — standard use of any in negative/interrogative context. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. much paper — much is used with uncountable nouns in negative/question context; possible but less natural here.
  • C. no paper — double negative with didn't; ungrammatical.
  • D. a few paper — a few is used with countable nouns; paper is uncountable here.
\[\boxed{\text{A) any paper}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which of the following options is the closest in meaning to the sentence below? She enjoyed herself immensely at the party.
options: She had a terrible time at the party
She had a horrible time at the party
She had a terrific time at the party
She had a terrifying time at the party
questions.explanation:
``She enjoyed herself immensely at the party'' — immensely means to a very great degree; she had a terrific time.
  • A. terrible time — negative; opposite meaning.
  • B. horrible time — negative.
  • C. terrific time — very enjoyable; matches immensely enjoyed. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. terrifying time — frightening; wrong meaning.
\[\boxed{\text{C) She had a terrific time at the party}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which one of the following combinations is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Match each word with its given synonym:
  • A. Acquiescence -- Submission — both mean acceptance without protest. \(\checkmark\) Correct pair.
  • B. Wheedle -- Roundabout — wheedle means to coax/cajole; roundabout means indirect. Not synonymous. Incorrect pair.
  • C. Flippancy -- Lightness — both mean treating serious things carelessly. \(\checkmark\) Correct pair.
  • D. Profligate -- Extravagant — profligate means recklessly wasteful; extravagant means spending excessively. Very close in meaning. \(\checkmark\) Correct.
\[\boxed{\text{B) Wheedle -- Roundabout}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Based on the given statements, select the most appropriate option to solve the given question. If two floors in a certain building are 9 feet apart, how many steps are there in a set of stairs that extends from the first floor to the second floor of the building? Statements:
  • I. Each step is 3/4 foot high.
  • II. Each step is 1 foot wide.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I and II together are not sufficient.
questions.explanation:
The question asks how many steps span 9 feet (first to second floor height).
  • Statement I: Each step is 3/4 foot high. Number of steps \(= 9 \div (3/4) = 12\). This alone gives a unique answer. \(\checkmark\)
  • Statement II: Each step is 1 foot wide. Width is irrelevant to counting the number of steps needed to cover a vertical height. Not sufficient alone.
\[\boxed{\text{A) Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Select the alternative meaning of the underlined part of the sentence. The chain snatchers <u>took to their heels</u> when the police party arrived.
options: took shelter in a thick jungle
questions.explanation:
``Took to their heels'' is an idiom meaning to run away quickly.
  • A. took shelter in a thick jungle — hiding, not fleeing.
  • B. open indiscriminate fire — attacking, opposite of fleeing.
  • C. took to flight — fled/ran away; correct meaning. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. unconditionally surrendered — opposite of fleeing.
\[\boxed{\text{C) took to flight}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: We our friend's birthday and we how to make it up to him.
questions.explanation:
The sentence requires two blanks: a verb for forgetting and a clause about not knowing how to make up for it.
  • A. completely forgot -- don't just know
    — don't just know is unnatural.
  • B. forgot completely -- don't just know
    — same issue.
  • C. completely forgot -- just don't know
    — completely forgot (adverb before verb) is natural; just don't know conveys helplessness. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. forgot completely -- just don't know
    — forgot completely is also acceptable but less idiomatic than C.
\[\boxed{\text{C) completely forgot --- just don't know}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the statement where underlined word is used correctly.
options: I write my experience in my <u>personnel</u> diary.
All <u>personnel</u> are being given the day off.
questions.explanation:
Personnel = staff/employees of an organisation (noun/adjective). Distinguish from personal = private/individual.
  • A. personnel jet — should be personal jet (private jet).
  • B. personnel diary — should be personal diary.
  • C. All personnel are being given the day off — personnel = all staff; correct usage. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. Being religious is a personnel aspect — should be personal aspect.
\[\boxed{\text{C) All personnel are being given the day off}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A generic term that includes various items of clothing such as a skirt, a pair of trousers and a shirt is
questions.explanation:
The expression describes a generic term for various items of clothing (skirt, trousers, shirt).
  • A. fabric — material/cloth; not a generic term for clothing items.
  • B. textile — woven material; broader than clothing items.
  • C. fibre — raw material; too basic.
  • D. apparel — a general term for clothing items; correct. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) apparel}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Based on the given statements, select the most appropriate option to solve the given question. What will be the total weight of 10 poles each of same weight? Statements:
  1. One fourth of the weight of a pole is 5 Kg.
  2. The total weight of these poles is 160 kg more than the total weight of two poles.
options: Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Either I or II alone is sufficient.
Both statements I and II together are not sufficient.
questions.explanation:
Find total weight of 10 poles.
  • Statement I: One fourth of the weight of a pole is 5,kg \(\Rightarrow\) weight of one pole \(= 20\,\text{kg}\); total \(= 200\,\text{kg}\). Sufficient. \(\checkmark\)
  • Statement II: Total weight of 10 poles is 160,kg more than total weight of 2 poles: \(10w = 2w + 160 \Rightarrow 8w = 160 \Rightarrow w = 20\,\text{kg}\); total \(= 200\,\text{kg}\). Sufficient. \(\checkmark\)
Either statement alone is sufficient. \[\boxed{\text{C) Either I or II alone is sufficient}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Out of the following four sentences, select the most suitable sentence with respect to grammar and usage:
options: Since the report lacked needed information, it was of no use to them.
The report was useless to them because there were no needed information in it.
Since the report did not contain the needed information, it was not real useful to them.
Since the report lacked needed information, it would not had been useful to them.
questions.explanation:
To determine the most suitable sentence, let us analyze the grammatical correctness and usage of each option:
  • Option A (Correct):
    The sentence structure is perfectly accurate. The dependent clause beginning with the conjunction ``Since'' correctly establishes the reason, and the independent clause completes the thought with appropriate pronoun usage (``it'' refers back to ``the report'').
  • Option B (Incorrect):
    The word information is an uncountable (mass) noun. Therefore, it must take a singular verb form (``there was no needed information''). Using the plural verb ``were'' is grammatically incorrect.
  • Option C (Incorrect):
    The phrase ``real useful'' uses the adjective real to modify another adjective (useful). Grammatically, an adverb must be used here to modify the adjective, making it ``really useful'' or ``very useful.''
  • Option D (Incorrect):
    The modal verb construction ``would not had been'' violates standard conditional tense structure. The modal verb would must always be followed by the base form of the auxiliary verb, which is have (i.e., ``would not have been'').
\[\boxed{\text{A) Since the report lacked needed information, it was of no use to them.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Extreme focus on syllabus and studying for tests has become such a dominant concern of Indian students that they close their minds to anything to the requirements of the exam.
questions.explanation:
The sentence describes students so focused on exams that they ignore anything unrelated to exam requirements — the blank requires a word meaning irrelevant or outside the scope.
  • A. related — opposite of what is needed.
  • B. extraneous — not relevant; outside the subject. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. outside — grammatically awkward without a preposition.
  • D. useful — contradicts the sense of closing one's mind.
\[\boxed{\text{B) extraneous}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair: Children : Pediatrician
questions.explanation:
Children : Pediatrician — a specialist who treats children.
  • A. Adult : Orthopaedist — orthopaedist treats bone/joint disorders, not specifically adults.
  • B. Females : Gynaecologist — gynaecologist specialises in female reproductive health. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. Kidney : Nephrologist — nephrologist treats kidney diseases (organ : specialist, not patient group).
  • D. Skin : Dermatologist — similar to C; organ : specialist.
\[\boxed{\text{B) Females : Gynaecologist}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The Tamil version of John Abraham-starrer Madras Cafe cleared by the Censor Board with no cuts last week, but the film's distributors no takers among the exhibitors for a release in Tamil Nadu this Friday.
questions.explanation:
Sentence: ``The Tamil version of ____ John Abraham-starrer Madras Cafe ____ cleared by the Censor Board with no cuts last week, but the film's distributors ____ no takers among the exhibitors for a release in Tamil Nadu ____ this Friday.''
  • Blank 1: ``the'' (definite article before a film title reference).
  • Blank 2: ``was'' (passive past).
  • Blank 3: ``found'' (found no takers).
  • Blank 4: ``on'' (on this Friday).
\[\boxed{\text{C) the, was, found, on}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: If ROAD is written as URDG, then SWAN should be written as:
questions.explanation:
ROAD \(\to\) URDG: find the shift for each letter. \[R(18)\to U(21): +3,\quad
    O(15)\to R(18): +3,\quad
    A(1)\to D(4): +3,\quad
    D(4)\to G(7): +3\] Each letter shifts by \(+3\). Apply to SWAN: \[S(19)\to V(22),\quad
    W(23)\to Z(26),\quad
    A(1)\to D(4),\quad
    N(14)\to Q(17)\] \[\text{SWAN} \to \text{VZDQ}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) VZDQ}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Alexander turned his attention towards India, since he had conquered Persia. Which one of the statements below is logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentence?
options: Alexander would not have turned his attention towards India had he not conquered Persia.
Alexander was not ready to rest on his laurels, and wanted to march to India.
Alexander was completely in control of his army and could command it to move towards India.
Since Alexander's kingdoms extended to Indian borders after the conquest of Persia, he was keen to move further.
questions.explanation:
The sentence states: ``Alexander turned his attention towards India, since he had conquered Persia.''
  • A. Would not have turned to India had he not conquered Persia — contrapositive of the sentence; logically valid. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. Not ready to rest on laurels — possible interpretation but not directly stated.
  • C. Completely in control of his army — not stated.
  • D. The extension to Indian borders is not mentioned in the sentence.
\[\boxed{\text{A) Alexander would not have turned his attention towards India had he not conquered Persia.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Most experts feel that in spite of possessing all the technical skills required to be a batsman of the highest order, he is unlikely to be so due to lack of requisite temperament. He was guilty of throwing away his wicket several times after working hard to lay a strong foundation. His critics pointed out that until he addressed this problem, success at the highest level will continue to elude him. Which of the statement(s) below is/are logically valid and can be inferred from the above passage?
  1. He was already a successful batsman at the highest level.
  2. He has to improve his temperament in order to become a great batsman.
  3. He failed to make many of his good starts count.
  4. Improving his technical skills will guarantee success.
questions.explanation:
The passage states the batsman lacks requisite temperament, not technical skills. Critics say until he addresses temperament, success will continue to elude him.
  1. He was already a successful batsman at the highest level — contradicted by ``unlikely to be so''.
  2. He has to improve his temperament to become a great batsman — directly supported by the passage. \(\checkmark\)
  3. He failed to make many good starts count — directly supported by ``throwing away his wicket several times after building a strong foundation''. \(\checkmark\)
  4. Improving technical skills will guarantee success — contradicted (technical skills are not the issue).
\[\boxed{\text{B) (ii) and (iii)}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The head of a newly formed government desires to appoint five of the six selected members P, Q, R, S, T, and U to portfolios of Home, Power, Defense, Telecom, and Finance. U does not want any portfolio if S gets one of the five. R wants either Home or Finance or no portfolio. Q says that if S gets either Power or Telecom, then she must get the other one. T insists on a portfolio if P gets one. Which is the valid distribution of portfolios?
questions.explanation:
Constraints:
  • U does not want any portfolio if S gets one.
  • R wants Home, Finance, or no portfolio.
  • Q: if S gets Power or Telecom, Q gets the other.
  • T insists on a portfolio if P gets one.
  • 5 portfolios for 6 people (one gets none).
Test option A: P-Home, Q-Power, R-Defense, S-Telecom, T-Finance:
  • S gets Telecom, Q gets Power ( Q's condition met).
  • R gets Defense — but R wants Home/Finance/none. Fails.
Test option B: R-Home, S-Power, P-Defense, Q-Telecom, T-Finance:
  • S gets Power, Q gets Telecom ().
  • R gets Home ().
  • U gets no portfolio (S has one) ().
  • P gets Defense, T gets Finance ( T's condition).
  • All conditions satisfied. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{B) R-Home, S-Power, P-Defense, Q-Telecom, T-Finance}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence. The official answered that the complaints of the citizen would be looked into.
questions.explanation:
``The official answered ____ that the complaints would be looked into'' — the blank modifies the verb answered and must convey a tone of respect.
  • A. respectably — means in a way that earns respect (reputation).
  • B. respectfully — means showing deference/respect to others; correct for the official's manner. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. reputably — means with a good reputation; unrelated here.
  • D. respectively — means in the stated order; grammatically inappropriate.
\[\boxed{\text{B) respectfully}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the statement where underlined word is used correctly.
options: The minister <u>insured</u> the victims that everything would be all right.
He <u>ensured</u> that the company will not have to bear any loss.
The actor got himself <u>ensured</u> against any accident.
The teacher <u>insured</u> students of good results.
questions.explanation:
Insure = to arrange financial protection; ensure = to make certain.
  • A. ``insured the victims that everything would be all right'' — should be assured (gave assurance).
  • B. ``ensured that the company will not have to bear any loss'' — made certain the company would not lose; correct. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. ``ensured against any accident'' — took out ensurance;
  • D. ``insured students of good results'' — should be assured.
\[\boxed{\text{B) He ensured that the company will not have to bear any loss}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which word is <u>not</u> a synonym for the word vernacular?
questions.explanation:
Vernacular = native or indigenous to a region; find the word that is NOT a synonym.
  • A. regional — relating to a particular region; close synonym.
  • B. indigenous — native to a place; synonym.
  • C. indigent — meaning poor/needy; NOT related to vernacular. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. colloquial — informal/everyday language; related to vernacular.
\[\boxed{\text{C) indigent}}\]
Key points
  • Indigent (poor) vs. indigenous (native) — a common confusion.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The word similar in meaning to `dreary' is
questions.explanation:
Dreary means dull, bleak, and depressing.
  • A. cheerful — antonym.
  • B. dreamy — pleasantly unreal; unrelated.
  • C. hard — difficult; not synonymous with dreary.
  • D. dismal — depressing, gloomy; synonym of dreary. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) dismal}}\]
Key points
  • Dreary \(\approx\) dismal, bleak, gloomy, dull.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Operators \(\square\), \(\diamondsuit\) and \(\rightarrow\) are defined by: \(a \square b = \dfrac{a-b}{a+b}\); \(a \diamondsuit b = \dfrac{a+b}{a-b}\); \(a\rightarrow b = ab\). Find the value of \((66 \square 6) \rightarrow (66 \diamondsuit 6)\).
questions.explanation:
We are given three operators defined as follows: \[a \;\square\; b = \frac{a - b}{a + b}\] \[a \;\diamond\; b = \frac{a + b}{a - b}\] \[a \rightarrow b = ab\] We need to evaluate the expression: \[(66 \;\square\; 6) \rightarrow (66 \;\diamond\; 6)\] Let \(x = 66 \;\square\; 6\) and \(y = 66 \;\diamond\; 6\). Step 1: Compute \(x\)
\[x = \frac{66 - 6}{66 + 6} = \frac{60}{72} = \frac{5}{6}\] Step 2: Compute \(y\)
\[y = \frac{66 + 6}{66 - 6} = \frac{72}{60} = \frac{6}{5}\] Step 3: Evaluate the final operator
Using the definition \(x \rightarrow y = xy\): \[(66 \;\square\; 6) \rightarrow (66 \;\diamond\; 6) = x \cdot y\] \[x \cdot y = \left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{6}{5}\right) = 1\] Alternatively, we can observe that for any valid \(a\) and \(b\), the operators \(\square\) and \(\diamond\) are reciprocals of each other: \[a \;\diamond\; b = \frac{1}{a \;\square\; b}\] Since the final operation involves multiplying the two results together (\(xy\)), the product of a number and its reciprocal is always \(1\). \[\boxed{\text{C) }1}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: If \(\log_{x} (5/7) = -1/3\), then the value of \(x\) is

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Fill in the missing value
questions.explanation:
To find the missing value in the bottom-most central circle, we evaluate the horizontal symmetry and patterns formed by the rows of overlapping circles. Let us analyze the grid row by row from top to bottom:
  • Row 1 (Top): \(6 + 5 + 4 = 15\)
  • Row 2: \(7 + 4 + 7 + 2 + 1 = 21\)
  • Row 3 (Middle): \(1 + 9 + 2 + 8 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 24\)
  • Row 4: \(4 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 15\)
Let us examine vertical column pairs centered around the middle value \([8]\): The central vertical axis contains the numbers: \(5\) (top), \(7\) (upper-mid), \(8\) (center), \(5\) (lower-mid), and the unknown blank circle \(x\) (bottom). Notice the balance of numbers symmetrically across the central vertical column:
  • Top row flanking elements: \(6\) and \(4\) sum up to \(10\). The center is \(5\) (\(\dfrac{10}{2} = 5\)).
  • Bottom row flanking elements: \(3\) and \(3\) sum up to \(6\). Following the identical structural average template established by the top row: \[x = \frac{3 + 3}{2} = 3\]
\[\boxed{3}\]

One of the parts may contain certain error or may not be acceptable in standard written communication. Select the part containing an error. Choose D as your answer if there is no error. The student corrected \(\underset{\text{P}}{\underline{\text{all the errors}}}\) that \(\underset{\text{Q}}{\underline{\text{the instructor marked}}}\) on \(\underset{\text{R}}{\underline{\text{the answer book}}}\).
questions.explanation:
The sentence provided is: "The student corrected all the errors (\(P\)) that the instructor marked (\(Q\)) on the answer book (\(R\))." To identify the error, we evaluate the sequence of actions and past tenses used in the sentence:
  • The sentence describes two sequential actions that happened in the past: the instructor marking the errors, and the student correcting those errors.
  • When two actions in the past happen at different times, the earlier action must take the past perfect tense (had + past participle), while the more recent action takes the simple past tense.
  • Here, the instructor marking the errors happened before the student could correct them. Therefore, part \(Q\) must use the past perfect tense: "had marked" instead of the simple past "marked".
Corrected Sentence: "The student corrected all the errors that the instructor had marked on the answer book." \[\boxed{\text{B) Q}}\]

questions.question: If \(a^2+b^2+c^2=1\), then \(ab+bc+ac\) lies in the interval
questions.explanation:
Given \(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} = 1\). Find the range of \(ab + bc + ac\). Using the identity: \[(a+b+c)^{2} = a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} + 2(ab+bc+ac) = 1 + 2(ab+bc+ac) \geq 0\] \[\implies ab+bc+ac \geq -\frac{1}{2}\] Upper bound: by AM inequality, \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geq ab+bc+ca\), so: \[ab+bc+ac \leq a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} = 1\] Therefore: \[ab+bc+ac \in \left[-\frac{1}{2},\;1\right]\] \[\boxed{\text{B)}\left[-\dfrac{1}{2},\;1\right]}\]
Key points
  • \((a+b+c)^{2} \geq 0\) gives the lower bound \(ab+bc+ca \geq -\tfrac{1}{2}\).
  • \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geq ab+bc+ca\) gives the upper bound.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
If \(x > y > 1\), which of the following must be true?
  1. \(\ln x > \ln y\)
  2. \(e^{x} > e^{y}\)
  3. \(y^{x} > x^{y}\)
  4. \(\cos x > \cos y\)
questions.explanation:
Given \(x > y > 1\). Check which must be true:
  1. \(\ln x > \ln y\) — since \(\ln\) is increasing and \(x > y > 1\): TRUE. \(\checkmark\)
  2. \(e^{x} > e^{y}\) — exponential is increasing, \(x > y\): TRUE. \(\checkmark\)
  3. \(y^{x} > x^{y}\) — not always true (e.g. \(x=3, y=2\): \(2^{3}=8 > 3^{2}=9\)? No, \(8 < 9\)). NOT always true.
  4. \(\cos x > \cos y\) — cosine is not monotone for \(x,y > 1\) (radians); NOT always true.
Only (i) and (ii) must be true. \[\boxed{\text{A) (i) and (ii)}}\]
Key points
  • \(\ln\) and \(e^x\) are both strictly increasing for all real \(x\).
  • \(y^x > x^y\) is not guaranteed for arbitrary \(x > y > 1\).

questions.question: Right triangle \(PQR\) is to be constructed in the \(xy\)-plane so that the right angle is at \(P\) and line \(PR\) is parallel to the \(x\)-axis. The \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates of \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\) are to be integers that satisfy the inequalities: \(-4 \leq x \leq 5\) and \(6 \leq y \leq 16\). How many different triangles could be constructed with these properties?
questions.explanation:
Right triangle \(PQR\) with right angle at \(P\), \(PR\) parallel to \(x\)-axis. Integer coordinates: \(-4 \leq x \leq 5\), \(6 \leq y \leq 16\). Counting choices:
  • \(P\) and \(R\) have the same \(y\)-coordinate (since \(PR \parallel x\)-axis): choose \(y_P \in \{6,\ldots,16\}\) — 11 choices.
  • \(x_P\) and \(x_R\) must differ: choose two distinct \(x\) values from \(\{-4,\ldots,5\}\) (10 values): \(10 \times 9 = 90\) ordered pairs, but since \(P\) and \(R\) are labeled, 90 choices.
  • \(Q\) has \(x_Q = x_P\) and \(y_Q \neq y_P\), \(y_Q \in \{6,\ldots,16\}\): 10 remaining choices.
Total: \(11 \times 90 \times 10 = 9900\). \[\boxed{\text{C) }9{,}900}\]
Key points
  • Right angle at \(P\) with \(PR \parallel x\)-axis \(\Rightarrow PQ \perp PR \Rightarrow PQ \parallel y\)-axis \(\Rightarrow\) \(Q\) has the same \(x\)-coordinate as \(P\).

The proportion of male to female students in each department is 5:4. There are 40 males in Electrical Engineering. What is the difference between the numbers of female students in the Civil department and the female students in the Mechanical department?
questions.explanation:
From the pie chart: Electrical 20%, Computer Science 40%, Civil 30%, Mechanical 10%. Male:Female ratio in each department \(= 5:4\). Total males in Electrical \(= 40\). Let total students in Electrical \(= n_E\). \[\frac{5}{9} \times n_E = 40
    \implies n_E = 72\] Total students in the college: \[N = \frac{n_E}{0.20} = \frac{72}{0.20} = 360\] Female students in Civil (\(30\%\) of 360): \[n_{\text{Civil}} = 0.30 \times 360 = 108\] \[F_{\text{Civil}} = \frac{4}{9} \times 108 = 48\] Female students in Mechanical (\(10\%\) of 360): \[n_{\text{Mech}} = 0.10 \times 360 = 36\] \[F_{\text{Mech}} = \frac{4}{9} \times 36 = 16\] Difference: \[48 - 16 = 32\] \[\boxed{32}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
The probabilities that a student passes in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry are \(m\), \(p\) and \(c\) respectively. Of these subjects, the student has 75% chance of passing in at least one, a 50% chance of passing in at least two and a 40% chance of passing in exactly two. Following relations are drawn in \(m\), \(p\), \(c\):
  1. \(p + m + c = 27/20\)
  2. \(p + m + c = 13/20\)
  3. \((p)\cdot(m)\cdot(c) = 1/10\)
options: Relations II and III are true.
Relations I and III are true.
questions.explanation:
Let \(p, m, c\) be probabilities of passing Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry. \[P(\text{at least one}) = 1-(1-p)(1-m)(1-c) = 0.75
    \implies (1-p)(1-m)(1-c) = 0.25\] \[P(\text{at least two}) = pm + pc + mc - 2pmc = 0.50\] \[P(\text{exactly two}) = pm + pc + mc - 3pmc = 0.40\] Subtracting: \(pmc = 0.10 \implies (p)(m)(c) = 1/10\) (Equation I) Using \(p+m+c\), \(pm+pc+mc\) identities: \[p + m + c = \frac{27}{20} \quad\text{(Equation II)}\] Relation I and III consistent with the given probabilities. \[\boxed{\text{D) Relations I and III are true}}\]

questions.question: Consider a function \(f(x) = 1 - |x|\) on \(-1 \leq x \leq 1\). The value of \(x\) at which the function attains a maximum, and the maximum value of the function are:

\(f(x) = 1 - |x|\) on \([-1, 1]\).

  • At \(x = \pm1\): \(f(\pm1) = 1 - 1 = 0\).
  • \(f(x) \geq 0\) on \([-1,1]\).

questions.question: In a triangle \(PQR\), \(PS\) is the angle bisector of \(\angle QPR\) and \(\angle QPS = 60^\circ\). What is the length of \(PS\)?
questions.explanation:
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(PS\) is the angle bisector of \(\angle QPR\) and \(\angle QPS = 60^{\circ}\). By the angle bisector length formula: \[PS = \frac{2qr\cos(\angle QPR / 2)}{q+r}\] Since \(PS\) bisects \(\angle QPR\) and \(\angle QPS = 60^{\circ}\), we have \(\angle QPR = 120^{\circ}\), so \(\cos(60^{\circ}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \[PS = \frac{2qr \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}}{q+r} = \frac{qr}{q+r}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) }\dfrac{qr}{q+r}}\]
Key points
  • Angle bisector length: \(PS = \dfrac{2qr\cos(\alpha/2)}{q+r}\) where \(\alpha = \angle QPR\).
  • \(\angle QPS = 60^{\circ} \Rightarrow \alpha = 120^{\circ} \Rightarrow \cos60^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

If the list of letters, \(P\), \(R\), \(S\), \(T\), \(U\) is an arithmetic sequence, which of the following are also in arithmetic sequence?

  2. \(P-3,\ R-3,\ S-3,\ T-3,\ U-3\)
  3. \(P^2,\ R^2,\ S^2,\ T^2,\ U^2\)
questions.explanation:
If \(P, R, S, T, U\) is an arithmetic sequence with common difference \(d\), check which lists are also arithmetic sequences:
  1. \(2P, 2R, 2S, 2T, 2U\) — multiplying each term by 2 gives common difference \(2d\). AP. \(\checkmark\)
  2. \(P-3, R-3, S-3, T-3, U-3\) — subtracting constant preserves common difference \(d\). AP. \(\checkmark\)

\[\boxed{\text{B) I and II}}\]

questions.question: The exports and imports (in crores of Rs.) of a country from the year 2000 to 2007 are given in the following bar chart. In which year is the combined percentage increase in imports and exports the highest?
questions.explanation:
To find the year in which the combined percentage increase in imports and exports is the highest, we first need to determine the total combined value (\(\text{Exports} + \text{Imports}\)) for each year from the bar chart. Step 1: Combined Totals
  • 2000: \(50 + 40 = 90\)
  • 2001: \(60 + 50 = 110\)
  • 2002: \(70 + 60 = 130\)
  • 2003: \(60 + 70 = 130\)
  • 2004: \(70 + 80 = 150\)
  • 2005: \(70 + 90 = 160\)
  • 2006: \(100 + 120 = 220\)
  • 2007: \(110 + 120 = 230\)
Step 2: Percentage Increase
  • 2001: \(\dfrac{110 - 90}{90} \times 100\% \approx 22.22\%\)
  • 2002: \(\dfrac{130 - 110}{110} \times 100\% \approx 18.18\%\)
  • 2003: No increase (\(130 \rightarrow 130\))
  • 2004: \(\dfrac{150 - 130}{130} \times 100\% \approx 15.38\%\)
  • 2005: \(\dfrac{160 - 150}{150} \times 100\% \approx 6.67\%\)
  • 2006: \(\dfrac{220 - 160}{160} \times 100\% = \mathbf{37.50\%}\)
  • 2007: \(\dfrac{230 - 220}{220} \times 100\% \approx 4.55\%\)
Conclusion:
The combined percentage increase is maximum in the year 2006 with a growth of \(37.50\%\). \[\boxed{2006.00}\]

questions.explanation:
The graph shows two segments: the positive \(y\)-axis (\(x=0\), \(y\geq0\)) and a line through \((0,0)\) and \((2,-1)\) for \(y\leq0\). Test option B: \(x = -(y-|y|)\) When \(y \geq 0\): \(|y|=y\) \[x = -(y-y) = 0 \implies \text{positive }y\text{-axis.}\ \checkmark\] When \(y < 0\): \(|y|=-y\) \[x = -(y-(-y)) = -2y\] Verify key points: \[y=0 \implies x=0\ \checkmark \qquad y=-1 \implies x=2\ \checkmark\] Both segments match the graph exactly. \[\boxed{\text{B) }x = -(y-|y|)}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Mr. Vivek walks 6 meters North-east, then turns and walks 6 meters South-east, both at 60 degrees to east. He further moves 2 meters South and 4 meters West. What is the straight distance in metres between the point he started from and the point he finally reached?
questions.explanation:
Let us analyze Mr. Vivek's path step by step by resolving his movements vectorially or geometrically. Let his starting point be the origin \(O(0,0)\). Step 1: First movement (North-East at \(60^\circ\) to East)
He walks \(6\,\text{m}\) in the North-East direction, making an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the East (positive \(x\)-axis): \[x_1 = 6 \cos 60^\circ = 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\,\text{m}\] \[y_1 = 6 \sin 60^\circ = 6 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}\] Position after first displacement: \(P_1 = (3, \, 3\sqrt{3})\) Step 2: Second movement (South-East at \(60^\circ\) to East)
From \(P_1\), he turns and walks \(6\,\text{m}\) in the South-East direction, making an angle of \(-60^\circ\) (or \(60^\circ\) below the horizontal) with the East: \[x_2 = 6 \cos(-60^\circ) = 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\,\text{m}\] \[y_2 = 6 \sin(-60^\circ) = 6 \times \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -3\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}\] Position after second displacement: \[P_2 = (3 + 3, \, 3\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{3}) = (6, \, 0)\] Step 3: Third movement (\(2\,\text{m}\) South)
From \(P_2(6,0)\), he moves \(2\,\text{m}\) due South (negative \(y\)-direction): \[P_3 = (6, \, 0 - 2) = (6, \, -2)\] Step 4: Fourth movement (\(4\,\text{m}\) West)
From \(P_3(6,-2)\), he moves \(4\,\text{m}\) due West (negative \(x\)-direction): \[P_{\text{final}} = (6 - 4, \, -2) = (2, \, -2)\] Step 5: Straight distance from start
The straight-line distance between the starting point \(O(0,0)\) and the final reached point \(P_{\text{final}}(2,-2)\) is given by the distance formula: \[d = \sqrt{(2 - 0)^2 + (-2 - 0)^2}\] \[d = \sqrt{2^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 4} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}\] \[\boxed {C){2\sqrt{2} }}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There are 16 teachers who can teach Thermodynamics (TD), 11 who can teach Electrical Sciences (ES), and 5 who can teach both TD and Engineering Mechanics (EM). There are a total of 40 teachers. 6 cannot teach any of the three subjects, i.e. EM, ES or TD. 6 can teach only ES. 4 can teach all three subjects, i.e. EM, ES and TD. 4 can teach ES and TD. How many can teach both ES and EM but not TD?
questions.explanation:
